lessons.title: Video contracts and resumable upload
lessons.summary: Keep control requests small while uploading video directly to durable storage.
lessons.body:
This case study uses an illustrative large upload-and-playback service; its capacity and timing targets are design assumptions, not measured company internals.

Video streaming is the classic "bandwidth is the system" design. The metadata service is a fairly ordinary CRUD app. What makes it hard is the **bytes**: petabytes arriving every day that must be transcoded, and hundreds of petabytes leaving every day that must reach phones on flaky 4G without stalling.

A strong answer spends little time on the metadata tables and most of its time on three pipelines: **upload → transcode → deliver**.

## Requirements

### Functional
- Creators upload videos (up to several hours long, many GB).
- Viewers watch on any device, with playback that adapts to their network.
- Search and browse metadata: title, description, thumbnails.
- Record view counts and watch progress ("resume where you left off").

### Non-functional
- **Playback start under 2 s**, and rebuffering kept to a tiny fraction of watch time. This is the metric that drives engagement.
- **Very high availability for playback.** A short delay in a new upload becoming watchable is fine; failed playback is not.
- **Durability**: never lose an uploaded original.
- Read-heavy: views outnumber uploads by many orders of magnitude.
- Cost matters a lot. Egress and transcoding compute are the main bills.

Clarify scope early. YouTube-style means a huge long tail of user uploads. A curated catalogue can support predictable placement, while a huge upload catalogue has a longer demand tail. These workload differences influence caching policy; either service can combine prefetch and demand-driven caching.

## API design

This is an illustrative endpoint contract, not a runnable HTTP request. Arrows distinguish responses from submitted fields.

```
POST /v1/uploads
  { title, size_bytes, content_type }
  -> { upload_id, upload_url }

PUT  {upload_url}
  Content-Range: bytes 0-8388607/...
  (GCS-style resumable chunks, e.g. 8 MiB)

POST /v1/uploads/{id}/complete
  -> { video_id, status: "processing" }

GET  /v1/videos/{video_id}
  -> metadata, status, thumbnails

GET  /v1/videos/{video_id}/play
  -> { manifest_url (signed, CDN),
       drm_licence_url }

POST /v1/videos/{video_id}/progress
  { position_s }
```

Two points matter here. First, the upload URL points straight at **object storage** (a pre-signed S3/GCS URL or a resumable-upload endpoint), so multi-GB bodies never pass through your API servers. Second, `/play` doesn't stream video. It returns a **manifest URL** on the CDN, and the player does the rest.

## Data model

| Store | What lives there |
|---|---|
| Sharded SQL | videos, channels, renditions |
| Object store | originals, segments |
| Wide-column / KV | watch progress, counters |
| Search index | titles, tags, captions |

```
videos(video_id PK, owner_id, title,
       status, duration_s, created_at)
renditions(video_id, codec, height,
           bitrate_kbps, manifest_path)
watch_progress(user_id, video_id,
               position_s, updated_at)
```

YouTube scaled its MySQL metadata tier by building Vitess, a sharding layer that is now an open-source CNCF project. Shard `videos` by `video_id` and `watch_progress` by `user_id`, because the access patterns are "load this video" and "load this user's history".

## High-level architecture

Follow the arrows as data paths; the drawing is not a deployment specification.

```
 Creator                          Viewer
    |                               |
    v                               v
+--------+   +-------+        +---------+
| Upload |-->| Blob  |        |   CDN   |
|  API   |   | store |        |  edge   |
+--------+   +-------+        +---------+
    |            |  ^               | miss
    v            v  |               v
+--------+   +---------+      +---------+
| Queue  |-->|Transcode|      | Origin/ |
| (jobs) |   | workers |----->| shield  |
+--------+   +---------+      +---------+
    |
    v
+----------+  +--------+
| Metadata |  | Search |
|   DB     |  | index  |
+----------+  +--------+
```

## Deep dive 1: the upload and transcoding pipeline

### Resumable upload

A 4 GB upload from a phone may be interrupted. Use a resumable protocol (Google's resumable upload API, tus, or S3 multipart). Offset-based protocols such as tus/GCS resumable upload report committed offsets. S3 multipart instead tracks an upload ID, numbered parts and their returned ETags/checksums; parts can arrive out of order and retry individually. A generic presigned S3 PUT does not implement a Content-Range resumable session.

When the upload completes, the storage service fires an event ("object created") onto a queue. Don't have the client call the transcoder directly. The queue makes the pipeline durable and lets you absorb upload spikes.

## Key takeaways
- The play endpoint returns a manifest URL; the CDN transfers the video bytes.
- Choose a resumable protocol with explicit committed-offset or part accounting.
- Separate video metadata, source objects, search and progress by their access patterns.

## Further reading
- [HTTP Live Streaming (Apple developer docs)](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/http-live-streaming)
- [Netflix Open Connect overview](https://openconnect.netflix.com/en/)
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
- [GCS resumable uploads](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/performing-resumable-uploads)
- [S3 multipart upload](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html)
- [Vitess overview](https://vitess.io/docs/overview/whatisvitess/)

questions.prompt: In an HLS-based video service, what does the `GET /videos/{id}/play` endpoint on your API servers typically return?

options.text: A playback manifest URL and any access or DRM details required by this service
options.explanation: Correct for this control/data-plane design. The API authorises playback and returns media-location information; the client obtains playlists and segments from delivery infrastructure. Signing and DRM depend on the access policy.

options.text: The video bytes, streamed from the API server over a long-lived HTTP response
options.explanation: Wrong. Streaming tens of Tbps through API servers would be ruinously expensive and slow. The API tier serves only small control-plane responses, and the bytes come from the CDN.

options.text: A WebSocket connection over which the server pushes segments at the right bitrate
options.explanation: Wrong. In HLS/DASH the client pulls segments and decides the bitrate itself. Server push over WebSockets would defeat ordinary HTTP caching, which is the main reason HTTP streaming won.

options.text: A single MP4 URL at the highest bitrate, which the player downscales locally
options.explanation: Wrong. This is progressive download. It can't adapt to the network, so a viewer on 2 Mbps 4G would stall constantly on a 15 Mbps 4K file.

questions.workedExample:
Separate the **control plane** from the **data plane**:

1. Control plane (your API): is this user allowed to watch? Which CDN node should they use? Here is a signed manifest URL valid for a few hours.
2. Data plane (CDN): the player downloads `master.m3u8`, sees the variants (480p at 1 Mbps, 1080p at 5 Mbps, ...), picks one based on measured throughput and buffer, then fetches 6 s segments one by one.

The API response is a few hundred bytes. The video might be gigabytes. Keeping them apart is what lets the API tier stay small while the CDN scales to Tbps.

questions.prompt: A sequential GCS-style resumable upload sends a 4 GB video in 8 MiB chunks, with only one chunk in flight. The connection drops near 3.1 GB. What should the client do?

options.text: The app restarts the upload from byte 0, because a partial object in storage may be corrupt
options.explanation: Wrong. Throwing away 3.1 GB on every dropout means a long upload on a flaky link may never finish. Resumable protocols exist precisely to avoid this.

options.text: The app asks the upload endpoint for the last committed offset, then sends only the chunks after it
options.explanation: Query the committed byte range and resume after it. Under the one-chunk-in-flight assumption, at most that 8MiB chunk may need retransmission. S3 multipart uses numbered part records instead of one committed offset.

options.text: The API server buffers the whole upload in memory, so the app can just carry on sending where it thinks it stopped
options.explanation: Wrong twice. Multi-GB bodies shouldn't pass through API servers at all, and the client can't know which in-flight bytes actually arrived, so it must ask the server for the committed offset.

options.text: The app re-sends the last 3.1 GB in parallel streams to make up time
options.explanation: Wrong. Those bytes are already stored. Parallelism helps with the *remaining* parts (S3 multipart allows it), not with re-sending committed data.

questions.workedExample: Ask the server which byte range is committed. Resume after that range, rather than trusting the client’s sent-byte counter. With one chunk in flight, interrupted bytes may need retransmission; a completed range need not be resent. GCS reports a persisted range, while S3 multipart recovery tracks numbered parts and ETags.

lessons.title: Video storage capacity
lessons.summary: Estimate original and rendition storage from explicitly dated upload inputs.
lessons.body:
## Storage grows with the catalogue

Uploading a video creates several storage obligations: the original, its delivery renditions, thumbnails and metadata, and the copies or erasure-coded fragments needed for durability. Count those separately. An original is not a delivery ladder, and a ladder is not a replica policy.

For an **illustrative** large platform, suppose creators supply 720,000 hours of video each day and originals average 10 Mbps. That is about 3.24 decimal petabytes of original payload per day. This is a chosen workload, not a current YouTube measurement or a universal bitrate for 1080p video.

| Budget input | Why it changes storage |
|---|---|
| Uploaded duration | More source hours add more original bytes |
| Source bitrate | Higher bitrate adds bytes even if duration is unchanged |
| Rendition ladder and codecs | Each retained encode adds another representation |
| Durability scheme | Replication or erasure coding adds physical overhead |
| Retention and deletion | Keeping everything makes the accumulated catalogue grow |

Measure rendition sizes on representative material. A complex sports clip and a static lecture need not use the same bitrate for comparable quality. Adding another codec for compatible devices may save delivery bandwidth while increasing stored bytes if the old codec remains available.

## Turn a storage total into a policy

Separate **daily growth** from **total retained storage**. A daily ingest estimate is not a one-time capacity requirement. Account for deletion, retention, indexes, unfinished uploads and temporary transcode outputs as well as completed media. Budget physical overhead once rather than multiplying the same replica factor twice.

Keep originals if the product needs future re-encoding. For seldom-watched renditions, compare keeping a ready copy with regenerating it after a request. Colder storage can reduce cost but adds retrieval delay and possibly retrieval charges; that choice must fit the playback promise. Monitor growth by object category so a temporary-output leak cannot hide inside an apparently plausible total.

## Key takeaways
- Convert incoming video hours into source bytes using the assumed bitrate.
- Model renditions and replication separately rather than treating a multiplier as measured.
- A dated upload figure is a planning example rather than current platform telemetry.

## Further reading
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
- [Netflix Open Connect overview](https://openconnect.netflix.com/en/)
- [YouTube 2019 official historical statements](https://youtube.googleblog.com/2019/?hl=ms)
- [S3 multipart lifecycle and unfinished uploads](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html)

questions.prompt: A service adds an AV1 ladder but keeps its originals and existing H.264 ladder. What should its storage plan assume?

options.text: The added ladder consumes storage even if compatible playback uses less bandwidth
options.explanation: Correct. New retained representations add bytes; delivery savings do not erase originals or older encodes.

options.text: Storage falls automatically because AV1 uses fewer bits per stream
options.explanation: Wrong. That compares encodes individually while ignoring that both remain stored.

options.text: The replica policy no longer matters
options.explanation: Wrong. Each retained object still needs the selected durability overhead.

options.text: Daily ingest is the entire lifetime storage requirement
options.explanation: Wrong. Retained data accumulates across days, subject to deletion and retention.

questions.workedExample: Separate source bytes, retained renditions, durability overhead and retention. An efficient extra codec can reduce delivered bytes for compatible viewers while increasing catalogue storage. Compare both costs before changing the ladder.

lessons.title: Video viewing and egress
lessons.summary: Distinguish peak delivery capacity from daily transferred bytes and regional demand.
lessons.body:
## Budget simultaneous viewing

Delivery capacity follows viewers watching **at the same moment**, their delivered bitrates and where they are. Daily active viewers alone cannot size a peak link: the same audience can watch evenly through the day or arrive together for a release.

An illustrative platform has 200 million daily viewers, averaging one watched hour at 3 Mbps. Spread evenly, that is about 8.3 million simultaneous viewers. If the chosen peak is twice that average, delivery approaches 50 Tbps. These are scenario inputs, not measurements of Netflix or YouTube.

## Peak capacity and daily transfer answer different questions

Peak traffic sizes links and delivery capacity. Total watched time and bitrate determine transferred bytes and the associated bill. Compressing the same viewing into a shorter busy period raises the peak without necessarily changing the day's payload. Holding bitrate and viewing constant while merely adding CDN sites does not reduce the bytes viewers consume.

Better encoding can reduce both peak bandwidth and total payload at the selected quality, but only for compatible devices receiving that encode. Retries, audio, protocol overhead and prefetch beyond what viewers watch add traffic beyond the simple video-payload model.

## Place capacity where demand occurs

Split the estimate by geography and busy hour. A worldwide average can hide one overloaded region. Test edge capacity, cache misses and origin fetches separately: an edge hit saves an upstream fetch but still sends media to the viewer.

Plan for failures and sudden popularity changes. A spare region or origin link is useful only if routing, cached content and authorised access still work when traffic shifts. The illustrative total motivates distributed delivery; it does not prove a particular number of sites or a universal data-centre limit.

## Key takeaways
- Peak egress depends on concurrent viewing rather than daily user count alone.
- Bitrate determines network bits; divide by eight when estimating byte storage.
- A CDN distributes distance and capacity, without a universal single-centre bandwidth cutoff.

## Further reading
- [Netflix Open Connect overview](https://openconnect.netflix.com/en/)
- [Content delivery network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Content_delivery_network)
- [Open Connect technical overview](https://openconnect.netflix.com/Open-Connect-Overview.pdf)

questions.prompt: The same audience watches the same total hours at the same bitrates, but a premiere concentrates viewing into a shorter busy period. Which budget changes most directly?

options.text: Daily payload must fall
options.explanation: Wrong. Total watched time and bitrate are unchanged in this model.

options.text: Replica storage must double
options.explanation: Wrong. Viewing times do not themselves add another stored media copy.

options.text: Peak delivery capacity rises even if daily payload is unchanged
options.explanation: Correct. More simultaneous streams require more instantaneous bandwidth.

options.text: Daily viewers alone now determine peak bandwidth
options.explanation: Wrong. Concurrency and delivered bitrate still determine the busy-period load.

questions.workedExample: Two viewing schedules can have equal daily viewer-hours but different peaks. The concentrated schedule stresses links and regional caches more intensely. Budget daily transfer cost and peak capacity separately, then add protocol overhead and failure margin.

lessons.title: Parallel transcoding and safe publication
lessons.summary: Version independent encode tasks and publish only validated winning outputs.
lessons.body:
## Compute follows the chosen quality target

Measure encoding work per source hour on representative content, codecs, presets and hardware. A core-hour is one processor core busy for an hour; the same core-hour count does not imply equal performance across machines. Daily work and available processing time inform fleet size, with headroom for retries and uneven task costs.

Keep the capacity model separate from completion latency. Enough total daily compute does not guarantee that one newly uploaded film becomes ready quickly.

### Split, transcode in parallel, stitch

A long serial encode can delay publication. To expose parallel work:

1. **Validate and probe** the file (container, codec, duration, corrupt frames).
2. **Split** it into chunks of a few seconds, cut on keyframe (GOP) boundaries using independently decodable boundaries (such as closed GOPs/appropriate random-access points), aligned across renditions. An arbitrary keyframe in an open GOP may still depend on other frames.
3. **Fan out** one task for each chunk-and-rendition combination to a worker pool. A 2-hour film in 4 s chunks across 6 renditions is about 10,800 tasks under these illustrative inputs, giving parallel work units; completion time depends on actual encoder throughput, available workers, input decoding and assembly.
4. **Assemble** the outputs into packaged segments and write the manifests.
5. Generate thumbnails, run content checks (copyright matching, safety classifiers) and extract captions in parallel branches.
6. Mark the video `ready` in the metadata DB.

A small chunk can be retried independently, but more tasks also add scheduling, metadata and assembly overhead. Measure both rather than assuming that finer chunks always finish sooner.

Model this as a **DAG** of tasks with a workflow engine. Every task must be **idempotent**, keyed on video/source version, chunk, rendition and encoding profile. Publish only complete validated outputs, using immutable attempt objects plus an atomic winning-result pointer or conditional writes. A deterministic path alone cannot stop a stale attempt overwriting a newer encode.

### The bitrate ladder

An illustrative H.264 ladder (not a universal recommendation):

| Rendition | Bitrate |
|---|---|
| 240p | 0.3 Mbps |
| 480p | 1.0 Mbps |
| 720p | 2.5 Mbps |
| 1080p | 5 Mbps |
| 2160p (4K) | 15 Mbps |

**Per-title encoding** chooses the ladder for each video's content and quality target. **Shot-based encoding** makes choices at scene boundaries. Static and complex motion footage can need different bitrates for comparable quality; measure savings on representative material. These techniques change the encode policy, not the requirement to publish compatible, complete segments.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Publishing a finished edition
> A printer can produce sections independently, but a publisher releases one chosen complete edition.
>
> **How it maps:** Chunk/rendition tasks correspond to separate print jobs; the ready manifest identifies the validated set selected for publication.
>
> **Where it stops:** Physical pages do not model stale network workers. The storage protocol still needs version checks and atomic winner selection.

## Key takeaways
- Chunk and rendition fan-out creates independently retryable work.
- Use independently decodable aligned boundaries; arbitrary open-GOP keyframes are insufficient.
- Publish immutable attempt objects through a conditional winning-result pointer.

## Further reading
- [HTTP Live Streaming (Apple developer docs)](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/http-live-streaming)
- [Netflix Open Connect overview](https://openconnect.netflix.com/en/)
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
- [HLS segment and playlist specification](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8216.html)

questions.prompt: A 2-hour film takes 6 hours in the current serial encode pipeline. Which design exposes parallel work and individually retryable units to reduce completion time?

options.text: Give the job a much larger machine (e.g. 192 cores) and run ffmpeg with more threads
options.explanation: A larger machine may help when the encoder scales, but it does not create separately retryable chunk tasks. Speedup depends on the codec, preset, hardware and threading; there is no universal 192-core ceiling.

options.text: Transcode on the fly at the CDN edge when a viewer first requests each segment
options.explanation: Wrong as the main strategy. Edge transcoding adds latency to every cold request, repeats work on every edge node, and needs heavy CPU at thousands of sites. It's occasionally used for niche formats, but not as the primary pipeline.

options.text: Split the source into keyframe-aligned chunks, fan out one idempotent task per chunk and rendition to a worker pool, then stitch the outputs
options.explanation: Split at independently decodable boundaries, align rendition segments and fan out tasks. Speedup depends on encoder scaling, compute capacity and scheduling/assembly overhead;10,800 tasks alone does not imply minutes.

options.text: Only produce a 240p rendition at first, because it encodes fastest
options.explanation: Partially useful (quick low renditions improve time to first watch), but on its own it gives viewers poor quality and doesn't solve the 6-hour wait for the full ladder.

questions.workedExample: Split work at independently decodable boundaries and align the required rendition segments. A failed chunk/rendition task can be retried without restarting the entire film. Benchmark chunk costs, scheduling and assembly rather than dividing serial runtime by task count. Validate outputs and atomically publish the selected complete version before marking the video ready.

questions.prompt: Your transcoding pipeline runs on spot instances. A worker is reclaimed halfway through encoding chunk 412 of video `v9` at 720p, and the workflow engine retries the task on another machine. Which design choices make that retry safe? Select all that apply.

options.text: Publish a complete validated object or atomically select an immutable attempt output, rather than expose partial data.
options.explanation: Correct. Readers (the packager) never see a partial segment, and an abandoned temporary object is harmless garbage to clean up later.

options.text: Each attempt writes to a fresh random filename, so two attempts never collide
options.explanation: Fresh attempt keys avoid collisions but alone do not identify the winning output. They can be safe when combined with atomic winner selection, as in option A; deterministic names alone do not guarantee idempotence or fence stale writes.

options.text: The video is only marked `ready` after every task in the DAG has completed
options.explanation: Correct. Marking ready early would publish a manifest pointing at a segment that doesn't exist yet. The DAG's final step is the single place that flips the status.

options.text: Workers increment a shared `chunks_done` counter when they finish
options.explanation: Wrong. A counter increment is not idempotent. A task that finishes, crashes before acknowledging and is retried would count twice, and the video could be marked ready with a chunk missing.

options.text: Include source and encode-profile versions in the task key, and use conditional completion/versioned output publication.
options.explanation: Versioned identities and atomic winning-result selection prevent stale attempts from replacing a newer encode. A fixed filename alone provides no such protection.

questions.workedExample: An interrupted multipart upload is not a completed object. Retry the versioned task, validate its full output and conditionally publish the winning result. S3 has no generic filesystem-style atomic rename; immutable object keys plus an atomic metadata pointer are an option. Track completed task identities rather than blind increments, and publish a ready manifest only after all required outputs exist.

lessons.title: Codec choices and encoding economics
lessons.summary: Compare extra encode cost with compatible watched-byte savings under explicit inputs.
lessons.body:
## Spending compute where views are

Assume a skewed popularity distribution for this design; measure the actual catalogue before allocating expensive encode work. A sensible policy:

- On upload, encode a fast H.264 ladder to target a short initial publication delay, validated by measurement.
- When a video crosses a view threshold, re-encode it in VP9/AV1. Potential bitrate savings and encoding cost depend on content, encoder settings and quality metrics; benchmark a representative corpus before choosing a migration threshold. Re-encode only when expected egress savings exceed compute, storage and operational costs for supported playback devices.

## An illustrative encoding break-even

Convert the delivered bytes saved per watched minute into an egress saving, then compare the extra encode cost. Suppose the alternative codec saves forty per cent of a hypothetical 2.5 Mbps stream and costs an extra $0.40 to encode. At a hypothetical $0.01 per GB:

```formula reference
T = C / s
where
T: compatible watched minutes needed to recover the extra encode cost
C: additional one-off encode cost, in US dollars
s: positive egress saving per compatible watched minute, in US dollars per minute
In words: a larger upfront encode cost needs more compatible viewing to repay it; a larger saving per watched minute repays it sooner.
```

Only compatible views save these bytes; added storage, licence costs and operational work can change the result. These inputs are hypothetical rather than a measured AV1 saving.


## Choose the population being priced

The watch-minute denominator matters. A video may be popular while most of its viewers use clients that cannot receive the proposed codec. Count only compatible delivered minutes when applying the saving. If the product keeps both encodes, the new rendition adds storage rather than replacing all existing files.

A useful decision record separates measured inputs from business choices: the observed quality comparison and encoder runtime, the device mix, the expected future watch minutes, the actual egress price, and the extra storage or operational cost. The reference model deliberately prices only the extra encode and saved egress. It is a scenario threshold to recompute when any input changes, rather than a universal rule that popular content should always be re-encoded.

## Key takeaways
- Measure codec savings on a representative corpus at the chosen quality target.
- Count views that can actually receive the codec, rather than all views.
- Compare total additional costs with repeatable egress savings before re-encoding.

## Further reading
- [Netflix Open Connect](https://openconnect.netflix.com/en/)
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)

questions.prompt: A trial codec saves delivered bytes at equal quality, but few viewers can decode it. What should decide whether to add that encode?

options.text: Total video views, regardless of device support
options.explanation: Wrong. Incompatible viewers keep receiving the older codec and do not produce the trial saving.

options.text: Encode cost alone
options.explanation: Wrong. A one-off cost must be compared with future savings and other added costs.

options.text: Compatible future watch time and measured savings, compared with all extra costs
options.explanation: Correct. Count the views that can receive the encode, along with compute, storage and operational costs.

options.text: A universal rule that CPU always costs more than bandwidth
options.explanation: Wrong. The balance depends on workload, hardware, prices and viewing volume.

questions.workedExample: Measure quality and bitrate on representative content. Estimate compatible watched minutes and price their saved bytes. Compare that benefit with the extra encode, storage and operational costs. More views help only when those views actually receive the new codec.

lessons.title: Adaptive playback and view aggregation
lessons.summary: Choose rendition quality on the client and aggregate popular-video counters.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 2: adaptive bitrate streaming

Progressive download of a single MP4 can't adapt to the network. **Adaptive bitrate (ABR)** streaming encodes the video at several bitrates, splits each into short segments, and lets the **client** choose a rendition per segment.

### HLS and DASH

- **HLS** (Apple) uses a *master playlist* (`.m3u8`) listing the variants, and a *media playlist* per variant listing segment URLs. Apple's HLS authoring specification recommends a target segment duration of 6 seconds.
- **MPEG-DASH** uses an XML *MPD* manifest with the same idea.
- **CMAF** standardises fragmented-MP4 segments, so one set of files can serve both HLS and DASH. This avoids duplicate segment copies when codec, encryption and player compatibility allow both protocols to share them; it does not universally halve total storage.

```
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1000000
480p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000
1080p/index.m3u8
```

Because segments are plain HTTP objects with immutable URLs, any HTTP cache or CDN can serve them. Cacheability and reuse of HTTP infrastructure are important practical advantages over specialised streaming delivery protocols such as RTMP.

### How the player chooses

- **Throughput-based**: measure how fast recent segments downloaded and pick the highest bitrate below, say, 80% of that. It reacts quickly but oscillates on noisy links.
- **Buffer-based** (Netflix's BBA research): choose the bitrate from buffer occupancy. With a nearly empty buffer, play safe. With a full buffer, go high. Buffer-aware policies can reduce oscillation; compare stability, startup and stalls on representative traces.
- Player implementations vary: many combine bandwidth estimates with buffer or switching constraints. Startup choices depend on their configuration and history.

Segment length is a trade-off. Short segments (2 s) offer more adaptation opportunities and can reduce live latency under the chosen buffering policy. They mean more requests. Compression may worsen if random-access spacing also shortens; segment duration alone does not prove a keyframe increase. Long segments (10 s) reduce request frequency but offer fewer switching opportunities.

## View counts and progress

Updating one popular video’s counter for every view can make that row a serialization bottleneck. Players emit heartbeats every few tens of seconds into a stream such as Kafka. A stream processor deduplicates (one view per session, with a product-specific minimum watch time and additional abuse controls), aggregates per video per minute, and writes counters. Displayed counts can lag by minutes. A lag of minutes may be acceptable for a display counter; billing or audit metrics may need another contract.

Shorter heartbeat intervals create more ingest work even when the audience is unchanged. Benchmark that event stream separately from the much smaller number of aggregated counter writes.

That is a workload to benchmark for the chosen partitioning and durability settings, and a sufficiently popular video can turn `UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1` into a single hot row taking tens of thousands of writes a second. Pre-aggregating in the stream turns that into one write per video per minute.

Watch progress can use a versioned KV record keyed by `(user_id, video_id)`. Define ordering across sessions/devices; client-clock LWW can let a delayed update overwrite newer progress, while taking the maximum position breaks intentional rewinds. It is debounced on the client so it isn't written every second.

## Key takeaways
- HLS and DASH can share compatible CMAF media while retaining their own manifests.
- Buffer-aware selection and switching hysteresis can reduce noisy quality changes.
- Aggregate deduplicated views rather than serialising every start on one hot SQL row.

## Further reading
- [HTTP Live Streaming (Apple developer docs)](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/http-live-streaming)
- [Adaptive bitrate streaming (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptive_bitrate_streaming)
- [Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_Adaptive_Streaming_over_HTTP)
- [RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8216.html)
- [Apple CMAF compatibility](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/http-live-streaming/about-the-common-media-application-format-with-http-live-streaming-hls)

questions.prompt: Your player uses a purely throughput-based ABR algorithm. Viewers on mobile complain that quality keeps jumping between 480p and 1080p every few seconds. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Switch to a buffer-based or hybrid algorithm that chooses the bitrate mainly from buffer occupancy, with hysteresis
options.explanation: Buffer-aware switching and hysteresis can damp oscillation. Tune them against representative traces; they do not universally eliminate all quality changes or stalls.

options.text: Make segments 1 second long so the player reacts faster
options.explanation: Wrong as a standalone fix. Faster sampling can make an unsmoothed controller more sensitive to noise; it does not add hysteresis. Shorter segments also increase request rate under the same buffering policy.

options.text: Remove the 720p rendition so there are fewer rungs to switch between
options.explanation: Removing a rung does not add smoothing or hysteresis and may make visible quality jumps larger. Validate the ladder and controller together.

options.text: Have the server choose the bitrate instead of the client
options.explanation: Moving the decision alone does not solve oscillation. A server-assisted controller could use client telemetry, but still needs a stable policy; server assistance does not inherently prevent cacheable segments.

questions.workedExample: A controller that reacts to the most recent download can alternate between high and low renditions as mobile throughput fluctuates. Buffer occupancy tells it whether a brief dip actually threatens playback, while hysteresis discourages repeated threshold crossings. Tune startup, switching and stall behaviour together against representative traces; no controller eliminates every stall.

questions.prompt: You must support both Apple devices (HLS) and Android/web players (DASH). Storage and CDN cache footprint are major costs. What packaging approach minimises them?

options.text: Store separate MPEG-TS segments for HLS and separate fMP4 segments for DASH
options.explanation: Wrong. Where compatible players and encryption can share fragmented MP4, separate media copies create avoidable storage and cache duplication; the effect on total storage and hit rate is workload-dependent.

options.text: Repackage on the fly at the edge from a single mezzanine file
options.explanation: Just-in-time packaging is legitimate, but adds execution and cache policy decisions. For compatible HLS/DASH playback, shared CMAF media can avoid duplicate media copies without requiring repackaging on every request.

options.text: Use only DASH and ship a JavaScript DASH player on iOS Safari
options.explanation: Dropping HLS does not satisfy the stated Apple/HLS requirement. Device, player and DRM support must be checked rather than assuming every platform can use the same DASH path.

options.text: Package once as CMAF (fragmented MP4) segments, and publish both an HLS playlist and a DASH MPD that reference the same files
options.explanation: Compatible CMAF segments can be shared by HLS and DASH manifests when codec, encryption and player support align. This avoids duplicate media copies for that ladder, not universally half of all platform storage.

questions.workedExample: For compatible players, codecs and encryption, both playlists can reference the same immutable .m4s objects. HLS has supported fragmented MP4 as well as MPEG-TS; separate duplicate media is not inherent to the protocol. Sharing files reduces duplicate packaging/cache footprint, but originals, alternate codecs and incompatible DRM combinations remain separate costs.

questions.prompt: A music video goes viral with 2 M people watching at once. View counts are stored as `videos.view_count` in the sharded MySQL tier, and each player runs `UPDATE ... SET view_count = view_count + 1` when playback starts. The shard holding that video starts timing out. What is the best fix?

options.text: Move the shard to a bigger machine
options.explanation: Wrong. Every increment to the same row takes the same row lock, so they serialise no matter how many cores you add. A bigger box buys little against a single hot row.

options.text: Re-shard `videos` by a hash of `video_id`
options.explanation: Wrong. The video already lives on exactly one shard, and it's one row. No sharding key spreads writes to a single row.

options.text: Send view events to a log such as Kafka, deduplicate and aggregate per video per minute in a stream processor, and write the totals
options.explanation: Correct under a delayed display-count contract. Aggregate deduplicated events and publish totals with retry-safe processor progress; reducing hot-row writes does not itself establish billing accuracy.

options.text: Cache the count in Redis and drop the database write
options.explanation: A cache-only count without a defined durability and retry contract can lose or duplicate updates. Redis can be configured for persistence, but the proposal still needs recovery, deduplication and any required fraud policy.

questions.workedExample: Every direct increment competes for the same row even if the database has many shards. A durable event stream can deduplicate view identities and aggregate updates before they reach that row. Persist processor progress and make output publication retry-safe; merely adding Kafka does not prevent duplicate totals. The display count can lag under its chosen contract, while billing or audit counts may need separate guarantees.

questions.prompt: For a live design that keeps the same approximate number of buffered full segments, what tradeoff follows from reducing segment duration from 6 to 2 seconds?

options.text: It cuts latency with no downside, because segment length only affects the manifest
options.explanation: Segment duration changes full-segment request frequency and can change buffer/packaging delay. Compression cost depends on codec dependencies and random-access spacing; not every segment or LL-HLS part must start with an independently decodable frame.

options.text: It can lower latency and triples full-segment requests. Compression may worsen if random-access spacing also shortens; LL-HLS parts can lower latency further.
options.explanation: It can reduce packaging/buffer delay under the stated policy and triples full-segment request frequency. Compression cost depends on whether random-access/keyframe spacing also changes. LL-HLS publishes partial segments for lower latency.

options.text: It increases latency, because the player must fetch three times as many segments before starting
options.explanation: Wrong. The player buffers a similar *number* of segments, so shorter segments mean less buffered time and lower latency.

options.text: It makes no difference to latency, which is set entirely by the CDN's cache TTL
options.explanation: CDN TTL alone does not set live delay. In the stated policy, keeping a similar number of shorter full segments reduces buffered time; encoding, packaging, network and player policy also contribute.

questions.workedExample: With a similar number of full segments buffered, shorter segments represent less buffered time and require more requests for the same playback duration. Reducing six seconds to two triples full-segment request frequency. Compression cost depends on whether random-access spacing changes too. Low-latency HLS parts can arrive before the parent segment completes; the actual latency still depends on encoder, network and player policy.

lessons.title: Video CDN placement and access
lessons.summary: Match catalogue popularity to proactive placement or tiered demand-driven caching.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 3: CDN strategy

A global viewing peak can exceed any one delivery site’s planned capacity. Place caches and capacity near demand, and test misses and regional failover as separate workloads.

### Netflix Open Connect

Netflix built its own CDN. **Open Connect Appliances (OCAs)** are storage-heavy servers provided free of charge to qualifying ISP partners and installed *inside* their networks or at internet exchange points.

- The technical overview describes Open Connect control and playback services in AWS, including authorisation and steering.
- OCAs store playable assets and serve requested video bytes over HTTP/HTTPS.
- Because the catalogue is curated and popularity is predictable, Netflix **proactively fills** OCAs overnight, during off-peak hours, with what each region is expected to watch tomorrow. Off-peak fills can use otherwise spare network capacity, and cache-hit video traffic can stay inside a participating ISP’s network; misses and other deployment arrangements still need upstream connectivity.
- At playback, the steering service returns URLs for the OCAs best placed for that client, ranked by health, load and network proximity.

### YouTube-style long tail

A long-tail upload service has uncertain demand for many new videos. An illustrative design can use **pull-through caching** in tiers; Google Global Cache documents caching popular Google content inside ISP networks:

```
client -> ISP edge cache (e.g. Google
          Global Cache)
       -> regional cache / shield
       -> origin object store
```

The head of the distribution (viral and popular videos) lives at the edge with workload-dependent hit rates. The long tail is fetched from regional caches or origin on demand. An **origin shield** can coalesce concurrent misses for the same cache key into fewer origin fetches; routing, eviction and failures determine the actual reduction.

### Security on the CDN

Manifests and segment URLs carry **signed tokens** with an expiry, so URLs can't be hot-linked forever. For this protected-media design, encrypt content using DRM such as Widevine, FairPlay or PlayReady, with keys from a separate licence server. For this protected-media path, cache encrypted segments; manifests, metadata and other CDN content need not be encrypted media ciphertext. Validate authorization separately from the shared object cache key.

## Bottlenecks and trade-offs

- **Egress cost** can dominate a delivery-heavy workload; measure it against encoding and storage. The levers are better codecs, per-title encoding, and ISP-embedded caches that avoid transit fees.
- **Transcode backlog** during spikes. Prioritise short videos and popular creators, and autoscale on queue depth using spot or pre-emptible instances, since tasks are idempotent and retryable.
- **Cold start for the long tail**. The first viewer of an obscure video pays origin latency. Consider prefetching likely opening segments into a regional tier, measuring useful hits against wasted storage and transfer.
- **Accumulating storage**. Move old, rarely watched renditions to colder tiers, and consider deleting high-bitrate renditions of dead videos and re-transcoding on demand.

## Evolving at 10x

- **Larger regional peaks**: push caches deeper into ISPs (the Open Connect model), and use multicast-like fills between caches.
- **Live streaming**: use LL-HLS or low-latency DASH with partial segments, an ingest tier that accepts RTMP/SRT, and real-time transcoding (no time to split and fan out a finished file).
- **Global metadata**: replicate read-mostly metadata to every region, with a single write region per shard.
- **ML everywhere**: predictive prefetch and quality-per-bit models (Netflix's VMAF metric) to tune the ladder automatically.

> **Content gap:** no reproducible encoder benchmark, CDN hit-rate measurement or current egress quote is supplied. Capacity, bitrate and cost calculations use explicit scenario inputs. Historical platform descriptions do not establish current internal implementations.

## Key takeaways
- Curated predictable demand makes off-peak placement useful; a long tail also needs misses.
- Origin shields coalesce requests, subject to routing, eviction and failure behaviour.
- Check viewer authorisation separately from shareable encrypted segment caching.

## Further reading
- [Netflix Open Connect overview](https://openconnect.netflix.com/en/)
- [Content delivery network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Content_delivery_network)
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
- [Open Connect technical overview](https://openconnect.netflix.com/Open-Connect-Overview.pdf)

questions.prompt: For an on-demand catalogue served through Netflix Open Connect, which workload properties make proactive off-peak cache filling useful? Select all that apply.

options.text: A curated catalogue allows a selected regional working set to be pre-positioned
options.explanation: A selected regional working set can be placed in advance. The fraction that fits depends on appliance capacity, rendition sizes and regional demand; long-tail services can also prefetch selected content.

options.text: Viewing popularity is predictable a day ahead from regional history and release schedules
options.explanation: When regional demand can be predicted, pre-positioning media can use spare off-peak capacity and reduce later peak transfers. Forecast quality and deployment costs determine the benefit.

options.text: Traffic is strongly diurnal, leaving spare network capacity overnight
options.explanation: Correct. Evening peaks and overnight troughs mean fill traffic can use capacity that would otherwise sit idle, keeping peak links free for playback.

options.text: Most content is live, so it must be pushed before anyone requests it
options.explanation: Wrong. The question concerns on-demand assets already available for placement. Future live media does not yet exist to be preloaded.

options.text: Viewers rarely seek, so only the first few minutes of each title need caching
options.explanation: Full episodes and seeking require placement beyond just an opening prefix. Actual OCA fill selects encoded assets according to appliance capacity and regional demand; it need not place every rendition of every title.

questions.workedExample: A curated catalogue, regional demand forecasts and off-peak network capacity make proactive placement useful. Open Connect describes ISP appliances and scheduled fill. Do not infer a fixed catalogue size, appliance capacity or universal hit rate from this pattern. A long-tail service can mix demand-driven caching and prefetch; these are not mutually exclusive platform categories.

questions.prompt: An obscure video is suddenly shared by a celebrity. Within a minute, 3,000 edge caches worldwide miss on its first segments at the same moment. Which measures protect the origin object store? Select all that apply.

options.text: Generating a unique signed URL per viewer that is also used as the cache key
options.explanation: If per-viewer token parameters enter the cache key, they fragment the cache. Configure authorization to run before cache delivery and normalize only authorization-only parameters; CDN defaults differ.

options.text: Prefetching the first few segments of each rendition into the regional tier when a video is published
options.explanation: If the predicted opening segments remain resident and usable, prefetch can avoid initial origin misses. Measure waste, eviction and incomplete placement.

options.text: Request collapsing at each cache tier, so concurrent misses for the same object wait on a single upstream fetch
options.explanation: Coalescing can share one in-flight upstream fetch for concurrent misses on the same cache key at a cache node. Retries and failures can still cause further fetches.

options.text: An origin shield (regional cache tier) between the edges and the origin
options.explanation: Shielding routes many edge misses through fewer upstream caches. Cache-key alignment, residence, coalescing and failures determine how many origin requests remain.

options.text: Lowering segment cache TTLs to a few seconds so caches stay fresh
options.explanation: Wrong. Segments are immutable, so they can be cached for a long time. Short TTLs would *increase* origin traffic by forcing repeated revalidation.

questions.workedExample: For an illustrative burst of 3,000 edge misses and 20 populated shield routes, coalescing can reduce origin fetches toward one per shield. Prefetched resident objects may avoid those fetches. Failures, evictions and routing can increase them. Validate each viewer’s authorization even on hits; do not remove identity-bearing cache-key differences unless the content is truly shareable.

lessons.title: Ride-sharing workload and state
lessons.summary: Distinguish high location-write throughput from transactional trip correctness.
lessons.body:
Ride-sharing looks like a booking app, but the core is a **real-time geospatial system**. Millions of moving points update every few seconds, and the hot query is "who is near this spot, right now?". Every trip also needs a strongly consistent state machine so a driver can't be sent to two riders.

## Requirements

### Functional
- Drivers go online and stream their location.
- Riders see nearby cars, request a ride and get a price quote.
- The system matches a rider to a driver. The driver accepts, and both see each other live.
- The trip progresses (en route → arrived → in trip → completed), then payment is taken.
- Prices surge when demand exceeds supply in an area.

### Non-functional
- **Match latency**: a driver offer within a few seconds of the request.
- **Freshness**: locations no more than about 5–10 s stale.
- **Correctness**: a driver is never assigned two trips. A trip is never lost or double-charged.
- **Availability**: the request path must keep working through a data-centre failure. A city with no dispatch is a city with no revenue.
- Location data is high volume but **ephemeral**. Only the latest position matters for matching.

## Three location budgets

Use a hypothetical peak of two million connected drivers reporting every four seconds. The resulting half-million updates per second describes **ingestion work**, not half a million trip bookings. A ping can replace a driver's previous position while a trip must preserve durable business history.

| Budget | What matters |
|---|---|
| Latest-position index | One recent position per connected driver, plus spatial-index overhead |
| Update stream | Reporting frequency, message size, validation and cell moves |
| Historical trail | All retained samples, retention duration, compression and copies |

At an illustrative 100 bytes per position, the latest raw records occupy about 200 MB before indexes, identifiers and runtime overhead. Keeping every ping grows far faster. Extending a peak ingest rate over a whole day is a stress scenario, not a measured daily volume.

## Spend precision where it matters

More frequent pings reduce nominal location age but increase network, battery and index work. They do not make GPS exact or guarantee a driver remains reachable. Use a freshness policy and exclude stale candidates. Coalesce superseded position updates where the product allows it.

Keep authoritative driver reservations and trip transitions separate from this refreshable index. A stale candidate may lead to an unsuccessful offer; it must not let two trips claim the same driver. Use atomic reservation guards and durable trip state even if the location tier favours availability during a partition.

Benchmark the busy-cell workload as well as the fleet total. A stadium can concentrate reads, pings and matching work on a few partitions even when total throughput looks healthy. Capacity planning therefore needs skew, reconnect bursts and degraded operation, not only an average number of writes.

## Key takeaways
- Latest location payload is small even when update throughput is large.
- Historical trail storage grows with all updates and needs its own retention plan.
- Peak factors and payload sizes are explicit workload assumptions.

## Further reading
- [H3: hexagonal hierarchical geospatial indexing (docs)](https://h3geo.org/docs/)
- [S2 Geometry library](https://s2geometry.io/)
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
- [Uber full-year 2024 company results](https://s23.q4cdn.com/407969754/files/doc_earnings/2024/q4/earnings-result/Uber-Q4-24-Earnings-Press-Release.pdf)

questions.prompt: A location service keeps only each connected driver’s latest position. Drivers start reporting twice as often, but their count and record sizes stay the same. What changes?

options.text: Latest-position records double in number
options.explanation: Wrong. Each driver still has one current record; the record is replaced more often.

options.text: Update work rises while the raw latest-record count stays the same
options.explanation: Correct. Reporting rate controls ingestion; driver count controls the number of current records.

options.text: Trip bookings must double
options.explanation: Wrong. A location ping is not a request for a new trip.

options.text: Retaining every historical ping costs the same as retaining one position
options.explanation: Wrong. Historical samples accumulate and need a separate retention budget.

questions.workedExample: Follow one driver: the new ping replaces their previous current position. More frequent pings increase validation, network and index work without adding current drivers. If every ping is archived, history grows faster even though the current-state index does not.

lessons.title: Ride location ingestion and recovery
lessons.summary: Stream sequenced positions into a partitioned soft-state index with durable trip contracts.
lessons.body:
## API design

This is an illustrative endpoint contract, not a runnable HTTP request. Arrows distinguish responses from submitted fields.

```
// driver app (persistent connection)
WS  /v1/driver/stream
  -> {lat, lng, heading, ts, session, seq}
     every 4 s (illustrative)
  <- {type:"offer", trip_id, pickup, ttl}

POST /v1/driver/offers/{trip_id}/accept

// rider app
GET  /v1/quotes?pickup=..&dropoff=..
  -> {quote_id, price, surge, expires_at}
POST /v1/trips
  {quote_id, pickup, dropoff}
  Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
  -> {trip_id, status:"matching"}
GET  /v1/trips/{id}   (or subscribe via WS)
```

The **quote** locks the price, including surge, for a few minutes. That way the rider pays what they were shown, even if surge changes a second later. The **idempotency key** on `POST /trips` stops a flaky network retry from booking two cars.

## Data model

This is a schema sketch: PK marks the primary key. It omits executable type declarations and migrations.

```
// in-memory, sharded by geo cell
driver_loc: driver_id -> {lat,lng,ts,
                          status,cell}
cell_index: cell_id -> set(driver_id)

// durable (sharded SQL / document DB)
trips(trip_id PK, rider_id, driver_id,
      status, quote_id, pickup, dropoff,
      fare, version, created_at)
drivers(driver_id PK, vehicle, rating,
        state, state_version)
```

Trips are sharded by `trip_id` (or by city, for locality). The trip row carries a `version` used for optimistic concurrency on state transitions.

## High-level architecture

Follow the arrows as data paths; the drawing is not a deployment specification.

```
 Driver app          Rider app
     |                   |
     v                   v
+-----------------------------+
|  Edge / WebSocket gateway   |
+-----------------------------+
   |            |          |
   v            v          v
+--------+ +----------+ +-------+
|Location| | Dispatch | | Trip  |
|service | | /matching| |service|
+--------+ +----------+ +-------+
   |   \        |          |
   v    \       v          v
+------+ \  +-------+  +-------+
| Geo  |  ->| Kafka |  |Trip DB|
|index |    +-------+  +-------+
|(RAM) |        |
+------+        v
          +-----------+
          |Surge, ETA,|
          | analytics |
          +-----------+
```

## Deep dive 1: ingesting locations

Drivers keep a persistent connection (WebSocket, gRPC stream, or MQTT) to a gateway. Persistent streams reduce per-message headers. HTTP keep-alive or HTTP/2 can also reuse TLS connections, so each HTTP update need not incur a handshake.

For each update, the location service:

1. Authenticates the driver and validates coordinates. Use a per-session sequence with a reconnect epoch to reject obsolete updates; use server receipt time for freshness and treat client time as untrusted. A plausibility filter can flag large jumps, but its thresholds need testing against GPS error and real travel.
2. Computes the driver's **cell id** at the indexing resolution.
3. Updates `driver_loc`. If the cell changed, it moves the driver between `cell_index` sets.
4. Publishes the update to Kafka for surge, ETA models, fraud checks and trip trails.

The in-memory index is **sharded by cell**, with neighbouring cells grouped onto the same shard where possible. Uber's dispatch system famously sharded geo-state across a consistent-hash ring (their open-source Ringpop library, using SWIM gossip for membership). Historical Ringpop is an example, not a claim about the current entire Uber stack. For this soft-state index, fresh connected-driver pings can rebuild locations after routing recovers. Four seconds is the nominal update interval, not a failover bound; disconnected drivers remain missing. This is a deliberate choice: **soft state** you can afford to lose.

## Bottlenecks and trade-offs

- **Hot cells**: a stadium can concentrate requests in a few cells. Finer cells help only if placement distributes the hotspot; batching adds computation as well as assignment opportunities. Apply measured capacity protection.
- **Consistency vs availability**: during a partition, this design can serve stale location candidates under an explicit freshness policy. Authoritative driver/trip mutations must refuse operations that cannot preserve assignment invariants. These are protocol choices, not automatic properties of a data type.
- **Straight-line vs ETA**: ETA calls are expensive, so pre-filter cheaply by cell and call routing only for the top candidates.
- **Mobile networks**: drivers drop out in tunnels. Use the freshness budget to exclude stale drivers; a degraded-mode policy might permit up to 30 seconds, but that explicitly relaxes the normal 5–10-second target.

## Evolving at 10x

- **5 M writes/s of location**: shard per city or region. Cities are natural failure and scaling domains, since a trip rarely spans two of them.
- **Multi-region**: active cities can be distributed among home regions with standby replicas. For each city, safe failover needs fenced ownership and a defined replication-loss policy. A driver phone may supply recovery evidence but cannot independently prove authoritative trip/payment state.
- **Richer products** (pooling, scheduled rides, deliveries) turn matching into a vehicle-routing problem. Batch windows and optimisation solvers grow in importance.
- **Edge compute**: run dispatch close to users for latency, and keep only aggregates global.

## Key takeaways
- Rebuild candidate locations from fresh pings while keeping trips durable.
- Atomic logical-operation deduplication prevents mobile retries from creating two trips.
- Hot-cell and region ownership plans require measured throughput and fenced recovery.

## Further reading
- [H3: hexagonal hierarchical geospatial indexing (docs)](https://h3geo.org/docs/)
- [S2 Geometry library](https://s2geometry.io/)
- [Optimistic concurrency control (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimistic_concurrency_control)
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)

questions.prompt: One shard of your in-memory location index crashes and loses all its data. What is the impact, and what is the recovery strategy implied by a good design?

options.text: Catastrophic. You must restore it from the last nightly backup
options.explanation: An old location backup cannot establish current availability. Recent replicated state may help recovery, but drivers still need freshness checks and new valid pings.

options.text: Trips in progress are lost, because trip state lives in the location index
options.explanation: Wrong in a good design. Trip state belongs in a durable, transactional store, separate from soft location state, precisely so a location-shard loss can't lose trips.

options.text: Rebuild the soft-state index from fresh pings once routing recovers, keeping authoritative trip/driver-assignment state in durable storage.
options.explanation: Nominal 4-second updates help recovery for connected drivers, but detection, routing, reconnection and network delays can extend degradation. Missing/stale drivers should be excluded until refreshed.

options.text: Replay the last 24 hours of Kafka location events into the new shard
options.explanation: Replaying a full day is unnecessary when only the latest valid location is needed. A recent compacted snapshot/log may help recovery; fresh pings follow the nominal four-second interval only after routing and device connectivity recover.

questions.workedExample: A shard crash removes candidate locations, not durable trips. Reassign ownership safely, accept fresh sequenced pings and rebuild the geo index. A lost or disconnected device may not refresh promptly; apply a freshness threshold. Optional recent-state replication or log replay can reduce degradation. No measured one-to-four-second recovery guarantee is available.

questions.prompt: A rider taps Request. The `POST /v1/trips` reaches the server and a trip is created, but the response is lost when the phone switches from Wi-Fi to 4G. The app retries automatically. What stops the rider ending up with two cars?

options.text: The client sends the same `Idempotency-Key` on the retry, and the server returns the existing trip for that key instead of creating another
options.explanation: Atomically claim the rider-scoped operation key and create its trip, validating the request fingerprint. Retries return the same recoverable operation; a separate non-atomic key write leaves a crash race.

options.text: The server rejects any second request from the same rider within 60 seconds
options.explanation: Wrong. This blocks legitimate cases (a rider booking for a friend, or cancelling and rebooking) and still returns an error rather than the trip the rider actually has.

options.text: The driver CAS prevents it, because a driver can only hold one trip
options.explanation: Wrong. The CAS stops one *driver* getting two trips. Two duplicate trips would simply be matched to two different drivers.

options.text: TCP guarantees the request is only delivered once
options.explanation: Wrong. TCP guarantees ordering within one connection. After a network switch the retry travels on a new connection, and the server can't tell it from a new request without an application-level key.

questions.workedExample:
Walk the timeline:

```
t0 POST /trips  key K1
t1 server: insert trip T1, save K1->T1
t2 response lost (network switch)
t3 retry POST /trips  key K1
t4 server: K1 exists -> return T1
```

The key is generated **once per user intent** (one tap of Request), not per HTTP attempt. Save the key and the trip in the same transaction, so a crash between them can't leave a trip with no key.

questions.prompt: Surge multipliers are recomputed every minute per H3 cell. A rider sees £14.00 (1.4x), taps Request 20 seconds later, and surge has risen to 1.8x. What should happen?

options.text: Honour the price via the `quote_id` returned with it, which is valid until its `expires_at`
options.explanation: Correct. Quotes lock the price for a short window (a few minutes). Surge can then be computed asynchronously and eventually consistently, while each rider's price stays consistent.

options.text: Charge 1.8x, because that's the current market price
options.explanation: The displayed unexpired quote is the contract in this scenario. Silently replacing it with a higher price breaks that contract; legal requirements depend on jurisdiction and product terms.

options.text: Recompute surge synchronously at request time so it's always exact
options.explanation: Wrong. Computing demand/supply over sliding windows and neighbours on every request is expensive, and still wouldn't match the price the rider was shown a moment ago.

options.text: Reject the request and force the rider to refresh
options.explanation: Wrong. It's poor user experience and causes extra request churn exactly when demand is highest. A quote with an expiry is the standard pattern.

questions.workedExample:
The design separates two concerns:

1. **Market signal**: a stream job recomputes cell multipliers about every minute under the stated policy.
2. **Customer contract**: the quote stores its identifier, rider, route, price and explicit expiry two minutes after creation.
3. Booking checks identity, route, expiry and any single-use rule before honouring that price.

After expiry, show a fresh price before confirmation. A KV TTL helps remove old records, but validate the recorded deadline explicitly; delayed eviction must not extend quote validity.

lessons.title: Geospatial candidate indexing
lessons.summary: Compare cell and tree indexes and distinguish graph neighbourhoods from metric radii.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 2: geospatial indexing

The query is "the K nearest available drivers within R km of the rider". A lexicographic B-tree on `(lat,lng)` is not a general efficient radius index. Spatial trees, database spatial indexes or cell mappings can support 2D searches.

### Geohash

Geohash interleaves latitude and longitude bits and base-32 encodes them. Shared prefixes mean nearby cells.

| Length | Approx. width × height near equator |
|---|---|
| 5 | 4.9 km × 4.9 km |
| 6 | 1.2 km × 0.6 km |
| 7 | 153 m × 153 m |

- **Pros**: simple, works as a string key in any KV store or DB. Redis `GEOSEARCH` uses a 52-bit geohash in a sorted set.
- **Cons**: the **edge problem**. Two points a metre apart across a cell boundary can share no prefix, so a radius search must cover every cell intersecting the search area and then filter by exact distance. The centre cell plus eight neighbours is sufficient only when the chosen cell size and search radius justify that coverage. Cells are also rectangles that distort with latitude.

### Quadtree

Recursively split a region into four until each leaf holds at most N points (say 100).

- **Pros**: adapts to density. Central London gets tiny cells and the countryside gets huge ones, which can help manage local density. Query work still depends on radius and the number of results.
- **Cons**: moving points can require structural maintenance. A quadtree may be held in memory or persisted; benchmark updates, skew and query cost rather than assuming every implementation is unsuitable for moving drivers.

### S2 (Google)

S2 projects the sphere onto a cube and orders cells along a **Hilbert curve**, which offers useful hierarchical spatial locality rather than a universal performance advantage over geohash's Z-order. Cells have 64-bit ids across 31 levels. A circle can be **covered** by cells at mixed levels. The cell-count limit and required accuracy determine the ranges to scan; a small covering may include substantial extra area.

### H3 (Uber)

H3 tiles the world in **hexagons** across 16 resolutions (0 to 15). Each step down is roughly 7 times smaller in area. Average cell sizes from the H3 docs:

| Resolution | Avg area | Avg edge |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | ~5.2 km² | ~1.4 km |
| 8 | ~0.74 km² | ~530 m |
| 9 | ~0.11 km² | ~200 m |

These are averages: because H3 projects from an icosahedron, hexagon area at one resolution varies by up to about 2x across the globe (excluding the smaller pentagons), so inspect actual local cell areas when density comparisons require precision. A sphere can't be tiled with hexagons alone, so each resolution also has 12 pentagons.

- A regular planar hexagon has six equally spaced neighbours. H3 approximates this geometry on a sphere; actual centre distances vary with projection distortion and pentagon boundaries. A square has edge neighbours and corner neighbours at different distances. This makes "k-ring" searches (all cells within k steps) and smoothing across neighbours clean.
- Uber built H3 specifically for surge pricing and supply/demand analysis.

> [!tip] What to say in the interview
> "I'd index drivers by H3 cell at about resolution 8 in an in-memory sharded store. For a request, I take a k-ring around the rider's cell, gather the available drivers, then rank them by road-network ETA, not straight-line distance." That names a real scheme, handles the edge problem, and shows you know crow-flies distance is misleading (think of a river with no bridge).

## Estimating a graph neighbourhood

Away from pentagons, a planar regular-hexagon approximation counts the centre and successive rings. This estimates query work; it is not an exact coverage guarantee for a metric pickup radius.

A regular planar hexagon model contains one centre cell, six first-ring cells and twelve second-ring cells: nineteen altogether. Real H3 neighborhoods can encounter pentagon distortion; a graph neighborhood is not a guarantee of covering a metric-radius circle.

A cell query still needs enough coverage, freshness checks and distance or ETA filtering. Average area does not prove that every point within a chosen circle is covered.

## Key takeaways
- Geohash needs boundary coverage and exact-distance filtering.
- H3 gives useful graph neighbourhoods with projection distortion and pentagon exceptions.
- Road-network ETA can differ substantially from straight-line distance.

## Further reading
- [H3: hexagonal hierarchical geospatial indexing (docs)](https://h3geo.org/docs/)
- [S2 Geometry library](https://s2geometry.io/)
- [Geohash (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geohash)
- [Quadtree (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadtree)
- [H3 cell statistics](https://h3geo.org/docs/core-library/restable/)
- [H3 graph traversal](https://h3geo.org/docs/api/traversal/)
- [Redis geospatial representation](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/geoadd/)

questions.prompt: You index drivers by geohash at precision 6 and answer 'nearby drivers' by looking only at the rider's own cell. Riders standing near cell boundaries report 'no cars available' while the map shows a car 50 m away. Why, and what's the fix?

options.text: Query all cells intersecting the required search area, including neighbors across boundaries, then filter by actual distance.
options.explanation: A 3×3 neighborhood suffices only when its geometry covers the desired radius at that latitude. Expand beyond immediate neighbors when necessary.

options.text: Geohash precision 6 is too coarse. Switch to precision 9
options.explanation: Wrong. Finer cells make the boundary problem *more* frequent, because more riders sit near an edge. Precision isn't the root cause.

options.text: Geohash cells overlap, so drivers are being double-counted and then removed
options.explanation: Wrong. Geohash cells tile the plane with no overlap. The issue is the opposite: there's a hard boundary that a single-cell lookup can't see past.

options.text: The geohash needs to be stored as an integer rather than a string
options.explanation: Wrong. The representation (base-32 string or interleaved integer bits) doesn't change which points fall in which cell, so it doesn't fix boundary misses.

questions.workedExample: A driver 50 m across a boundary is invisible to a single-cell lookup. Cover every cell intersecting the desired metric search region, fetch candidates, then distance-filter. Geohash widths shrink with latitude, so the equatorial 1.2 km × 0.6 km dimensions do not prove coverage everywhere. H3 gridDisk supplies graph-distance neighbors; pentagons and projection distortion mean it is not an exact equal-distance circle.

questions.prompt: Uber built H3 using hexagons rather than squares. Which advantages of hexagonal cells matter for surge pricing and supply/demand analysis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Regular planar hexagons have six equally spaced edge neighbors, which provides a useful approximation for local H3 smoothing.
options.explanation: H3 approximates this geometry on a sphere; actual distances vary with projection distortion and near pentagons. It does not make every direction exactly equal.

options.text: k-ring queries (all cells within k steps) approximate a circle well
options.explanation: Hexagonal graph neighbourhoods are approximately circular in a regular local model, which is useful for smoothing. They do not prove coverage of an exact kilometre radius on H3.

options.text: Hexagons nest perfectly, so each parent is exactly 7 children with no gaps or overlap
options.explanation: Wrong. Hexagons *can't* be tiled exactly by smaller hexagons. H3's children only approximately cover their parent (with a rotation between resolutions). S2's square cells, by contrast, nest exactly.

options.text: Hexagonal cells eliminate the need for any neighbour lookups
options.explanation: Wrong. You still need neighbours. Hexagons just make neighbour relationships uniform and cheap to compute.

options.text: Cells at a given resolution have roughly uniform area, so per-cell supply/demand ratios are comparable
options.explanation: Comparable local hexagon areas can help analysis, but actual areas vary with projection and near pentagons. Inspect the relevant cells or normalise counts by area where precision matters.

questions.workedExample: Hexagonal graph neighborhoods are useful for local smoothing and approximately circular candidate regions. H3 has projection distortion and twelve pentagons per resolution, so actual distances/areas vary. The roughly 2× global area ratio refers to hexagons only. Parent-child logical hierarchy is exact, while geometric containment is approximate.

questions.prompt: An H3 gridDisk search covers two graph rings. Can its estimated total area prove that every driver within a particular kilometre radius is included?

options.text: Yes, equal area means equal boundaries
options.explanation: Wrong. Regions can have the same area and different shapes or gaps relative to a desired circle.

options.text: Yes, all H3 cells are exact regular hexagons
options.explanation: Wrong. Projection distortion and pentagons affect actual geometry.

options.text: No; cover the intended metric region and distance-filter candidates
options.explanation: Correct. Graph steps and area estimates do not prove metric-radius coverage.

options.text: No neighboring cells are needed if the centre cell is precise enough
options.explanation: Wrong. A nearby driver can lie immediately across its boundary.

questions.workedExample: The graph query follows cell adjacency. The pickup requirement is expressed in physical distance. Check that the selected cells cover that distance region, expand when necessary and filter candidates by actual distance or ETA. Cell-count arithmetic alone cannot establish coverage.

lessons.title: Matching, offers and price quotes
lessons.summary: Coordinate driver reservations while treating location and surge signals as separate policies.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 3: matching

### Candidate generation and ranking
1. Use a cell neighborhood large enough for the intended search area; a fixed graph radius is only an approximation to a metric radius. Expand candidates as needed and filter/rank by actual distance or ETA.
2. Filter to `status = available` and to the right vehicle type.
3. Ask the **ETA service** (routing on a road graph with live traffic) for the top ~10 by straight-line distance.
4. Rank by ETA, plus factors such as acceptance rate and keeping drivers' earnings fair.

### Offering without double-booking
The crucial correctness property is that **a driver holds at most one offer or trip**. Make driver state an explicit state machine with a compare-and-set:

This SQL fragment uses driver ID and version parameters bound by the application. The surrounding transaction must coordinate the corresponding trip reservation.

```sql
-- Compete only for this available version.
UPDATE drivers
SET state='offered', state_version=:v+1
WHERE driver_id=:driver
  AND state='available'
  AND state_version=:v;
```

Only one dispatcher can win that CAS. The offer goes out with a TTL (say 15 s). Bind the offer to a unique offer ID and epoch. A timeout may release only that same still-pending offer; it must not undo a later acceptance or offer. Acceptance must atomically validate and update the driver reservation and trip, or use a recoverable protocol preserving both invariants. Two unrelated CAS operations alone are insufficient.

### Greedy versus batched matching
Greedy matching (each request immediately takes the nearest driver) makes a locally attractive choice that can be globally suboptimal. Two riders a block apart can each grab the driver better suited to the other. An illustrative **batched matching** design collects requests for a short window (say 1–2 s), builds a cost matrix of ETAs, and solves the assignment problem (for example, Hungarian-style algorithms). This optimises the chosen estimated assignment cost, while adding delay and computation. Measure whether the net pickup-time benefit survives those costs and estimation errors.

## Deep dive 4: surge pricing

Surge balances the market. Higher prices can influence supply and demand; the size and timing of the response are empirical and market-dependent.

One illustrative surge policy is:

1. A stream job (Flink or Kafka Streams) consumes ride requests (demand) and available-driver pings (supply).
2. Every ~1 minute, per H3 cell (around resolution 7–8), compute demand/supply over an overlapping stream time window.
