lessons.title: Payment workload and correctness boundaries
lessons.summary: Size ledger traffic while distinguishing operational, retention and provider assumptions.
lessons.body:
A payment system must distinguish permitted delays in display state from conflicting authoritative money movements. A duplicate charge is a furious customer and a chargeback. A lost capture is lost revenue. A ledger that doesn't balance is a regulatory problem.

The honest framing in an interview is that the network can't give you exactly-once, so you aim for **effectively-once operations within explicit provider contracts** using idempotency keys, state machines, an immutable double-entry ledger, and reconciliation against external truth.

## Requirements

Assume a marketplace (think ride-hailing or e-commerce). Customers pay, the platform takes a fee, and sellers are paid out.

### Functional
- Accept card and wallet payments through one or more **PSPs** (Payment Service Providers such as Stripe, Adyen or Braintree).
- Authorise, capture, refund (full or partial), and handle chargebacks.
- Keep a **ledger** of who owes whom.
- Pay sellers on a schedule (daily payouts to bank accounts).
- Reconcile with PSP settlement reports and bank statements.

### Non-functional
- **Correctness over availability**. It's better to fail a payment cleanly than to double-charge.
- **Idempotency** on every mutating operation, end to end.
- **Auditability**: an immutable history and the ability to explain every penny.
- **Security**: minimise PCI DSS scope (never store raw card numbers).
- Latency target for an uncomplicated card request: 1–3 s as an illustrative product budget. Authentication, asynchronous methods and settlement can take much longer.

## Count operations, not only payments

Use ten million daily payments as an illustrative workload, not a provider benchmark. A payment may create several ledger postings, state changes and provider calls. Refunds, disputes and retries add work after the initial checkout, while reconciliation reads old records.

Raw payload estimates exclude indexes, transaction records, replication and backups. The number of entries depends on the accounting policy: a gross revenue posting with a separate provider fee differs from a net presentation. Benchmark the actual transaction shape and hot accounts before inferring a safe payment rate.

## Correctness work survives the busy hour

A timeout can leave an operation unresolved even after the customer has left. Preserve its stable identity, provider reference and recoverable state. More retries do not remove ambiguity, and expired idempotency keys can make a blind resubmission unsafe.

Distinguish accepting an operation from completing it. Cleanly rejecting new work may protect the system; an in-flight UNKNOWN payment still needs reconciliation. Monitor ageing unresolved operations and durable relay backlogs as well as successful requests per second.

## Retention is a separate requirement

An append-only ledger accumulates history. Retention depends on record type, jurisdiction and the product's obligations; this architecture supplies no universal number of years. Specify required retention and retrieval before selecting hot storage, archival partitions and deletion policies. Keep those decisions separate from a chosen daily traffic estimate.

The central engineering difficulty is partial failure: a provider succeeds but its response is lost, an event arrives twice, or two paths try to post the same capture. Atomic local state, provider contracts and external reconciliation address different parts of that problem.

> **Content gap:** no production capacity benchmark or jurisdiction-complete financial compliance analysis is supplied. The schema, accounting policy and timing targets are illustrative; they are not a complete regulated payments implementation.

## Key takeaways
- Payment capacity is a transaction-shape and contention benchmark.
- Retention periods depend on jurisdiction and record type.
- Effectively-once external operations require explicit provider contracts and reconciliation.

## Further reading
- [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (Stripe)](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)
- [Idempotent requests (Stripe API docs)](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)
- [The Payment Intents API (Stripe docs)](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/payment-intents)
- [Accounting for developers, part I (Modern Treasury)](https://www.moderntreasury.com/journal/accounting-for-developers-part-i)

questions.prompt: A payment capacity estimate counts only raw ledger-entry bytes. What is missing before choosing the database configuration?

options.text: The full transaction shape, indexes, copies, contention, recovery work and retention
options.explanation: Correct. A payload total does not establish sustainable throughput or physical capacity.

options.text: Nothing; raw byte volume proves every database can keep up
options.explanation: Wrong. Latency and correctness depend on the actual operations and failure model.

options.text: Only the size of a customer’s card number
options.explanation: Wrong. Hosted payment collection avoids storing raw card details; it does not remove ledger overhead.

options.text: A universal retention period shared by every jurisdiction and record type
options.explanation: Wrong. Retention must follow the applicable requirements, not an invented universal number.

questions.workedExample: One checkout can cause several postings, provider calls and later refunds or disputes. Benchmark the real transaction and hot accounts, then add physical overhead and required history. Preserve unresolved operations for recovery even when the busy hour has ended.

lessons.title: Payment amounts and idempotency
lessons.summary: Represent money exactly and keep one operation identity through every retry boundary.
lessons.body:
## API design

This is an illustrative endpoint contract, not a runnable HTTP request. Arrows distinguish responses from submitted fields.

```
POST /v1/payments
  Idempotency-Key: 6f1c...
  { amount: 2350, currency: "GBP",
    customer_id, payment_method_token,
    order_id, capture: "automatic" }
  -> { payment_id, status }

POST /v1/payments/{id}/capture
  Idempotency-Key: ...
POST /v1/payments/{id}/refunds
  Idempotency-Key: ...
  { amount: 500 }

POST /webhooks/psp/{provider}
  (signed by PSP)
GET  /v1/accounts/{id}/balance
```

Three rules:

- **Amounts are integers in minor units** (2,350 pence represents £23.50) with an explicit currency. A minor unit is the currency's smallest subdivision, such as the penny for pounds sterling:

Store 2,350 whole pence for £23.50. The currency identifies what a minor unit means; display conversion must not silently assume that every currency has two decimal places.

Consult the currency standard and the deployed provider’s amount rules rather than assuming two decimal places. A provider can impose special charge or payout conventions that differ from a simple currency-exponent conversion. Avoid binary floating-point for exact money amounts: many decimal fractions are not exactly representable. Exact decimal types are also valid when precision and rounding are specified; IEEE 754 includes decimal formats.
- **`payment_method_token`, never a card number.** The card is collected by the PSP's hosted fields or SDK and swapped for a token, which reduces PCI DSS scope; the merchant still has compliance obligations that depend on the integration.
- **Every mutating call takes an idempotency key.**

## Data model

This is a schema sketch: PK marks the primary key. It omits executable type declarations and migrations.

```
payments(payment_id PK, order_id,
  amount, currency, status, psp,
  psp_payment_ref, version, created_at)

idempotency_keys(key, merchant_id, PK both
  request_hash, status, response,
  locked_until, created_at)

ledger_entries(entry_id PK, txn_id,
  account_id, amount (signed, minor),
  currency, created_at)   -- append-only
ledger_txns(txn_id PK, type,
  ref_id UNIQUE, created_at)

accounts(account_id PK, type, currency,
  balance, version)       -- materialised

psp_events(provider, event_id, PK both
  payload, processed_at)
```

## High-level architecture

Follow the arrows as data paths; the drawing is not a deployment specification.

```
 Client (PSP SDK tokenises card)
        |
        v
+---------------+   +--------------+
| Payments API  |-->| Idempotency  |
+---------------+   | store        |
        |           +--------------+
        v
+---------------+   +--------------+
| Payment       |-->| PSP adapter  |
| orchestrator  |   | (Stripe,     |
| (state mach.) |<--| Adyen, ...)  |
+---------------+   +--------------+
        |   ^  webhooks    |
        v   +--------------+
+---------------+   +--------------+
| Ledger        |   | Reconciler   |
| (double-entry)|<->| (daily files)|
+---------------+   +--------------+
        |
        v
  Payouts -> bank rails
```

## Deep dive 1: idempotency keys

A mobile client sends `POST /payments`, the response is lost to a timeout, and the client retries. Without protection, the customer is charged twice. The fix, popularised by Stripe:

1. The client generates a **unique key per logical operation** (a UUID) and reuses it on every retry of that operation.
2. The server does an `INSERT` into `idempotency_keys` with status `in_progress` and a hash of the request body.
   - If the insert succeeds, process the request.
   - First check merchant/operation scope and request fingerprint; if they match and the key is **completed**, return the stored result.
   - If the key exists and is **in progress**, return `409` (or wait). A concurrent duplicate must not run in parallel.
   - If the key exists with a **different request hash**, return `422`. The same key was reused for a different operation, which is a client bug.
3. On completion, store the response and mark the key completed. Do this in the same transaction as the business state change wherever possible.
4. Expire keys after a window. For Stripe API v1, a key may be pruned once it is at least 24 hours old; reusing a pruned key makes a new request. API v1 replays the first executed status/body, including server errors, while API v2 has different retry semantics. Check the deployed endpoint contract.

The 409 versus 422 split above matches the IETF's Internet-Draft for an `Idempotency-Key` HTTP header. As checked on 3 November 2026, revision 08 is an active Internet-Draft published on 22 October 2026; it is not an RFC. These status codes remain a convention to document for your own API.

Idempotency has to go **all the way down**. When your orchestrator calls the PSP, pass a deterministic idempotency key derived from your payment id, for example `pay_123:authorise`. If your own retry of the PSP call happens after a crash, the PSP can deduplicate it within its documented endpoint, parameter and retention contract. After key expiry, reconcile rather than blindly resubmitting an unresolved payment. Use a distinct stable operation ID for each capture/refund, including multiple partial refunds.

## Key takeaways
- Use explicit currency and exact minor-unit or decimal arithmetic.
- Atomically claim scoped operation keys and reject mismatched request fingerprints.
- Provider retention and operation scope constrain safe same-key retries.

## Further reading
- [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (Stripe)](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)
- [Idempotent requests (Stripe API docs)](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)
- [The Payment Intents API (Stripe docs)](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/payment-intents)
- [Stripe currency amount rules](https://docs.stripe.com/currencies)
- [Payment integration security](https://docs.stripe.com/security/guide)
- [Current Idempotency-Key draft status](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/)

questions.prompt: Why should a payment system store `amount: 2350, currency: "GBP"` rather than `amount: 23.50`?

options.text: Binary floating point can't represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift (even adding small decimal fractions can show a binary rounding artefact). Integer minor units are exact, and the explicit currency says what a unit means
options.explanation: Correct. Financial arithmetic must be exact and auditable. Integers in minor units (pence, cents), or a fixed-point decimal type, avoid rounding drift. Currency matters because minor units differ: JPY has 0 decimal places and BHD has 3.

options.text: Integers take less storage than floats
options.explanation: Wrong. Both are typically 8 bytes. Storage isn't the reason. Exactness is.

options.text: JSON can't encode decimal numbers
options.explanation: Wrong. JSON can encode 23.50, but most parsers turn it into an IEEE 754 double, which reintroduces the precision problem. That's a reason to avoid it, but JSON itself isn't the limitation.

options.text: PSPs reject decimal amounts for security reasons
options.explanation: Wrong. Many PSP APIs (Stripe, for example) do take integer minor units, but for precision and unambiguity, not security.

questions.workedExample: For JavaScript Number (binary64), `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`. Repeated naive addition of 0.01 can accumulate error; exact results depend on the summation algorithm. Integer pence give `10 + 20 = 30` exactly within the integer range. Exact decimal types are another option with explicit precision and rounding. Currency exponents and PSP-specific amount rules must be checked: GBP uses pence, JPY whole yen and BHD fils.

questions.prompt: A client sends `POST /payments` with `Idempotency-Key: K1`. While the first request is still processing (waiting on the PSP), a retry with the same key arrives at another server. What should that server do?

options.text: Process it too. Idempotency only matters after the first request finishes
options.explanation: Wrong. Concurrent duplicates are the most dangerous case. Two in-flight requests could each call the PSP and create two charges before either stores a result.

options.text: Generate a new key K2 and process it as a fresh payment
options.explanation: A new key would identify a new logical operation and defeat deduplication. Servers may generate stable operation keys in other designs; the error here is generating a fresh key for a retry.

options.text: See that K1 exists in state `in_progress` and return 409 Conflict (or block until the first completes), without starting a second execution
options.explanation: Correct. The key row is inserted atomically as `in_progress` before any side effect, so the duplicate can't start a parallel execution. Once the first completes, retries get the stored response.

options.text: Return the stored response, which will be empty
options.explanation: Wrong. There's no stored response yet. Returning an empty or placeholder success would mislead the client into thinking the payment completed.

questions.workedExample: Atomically insert a merchant-scoped key, operation scope and request fingerprint. On conflict, validate the fingerprint before returning a completed result or 409 for in-progress work. A recoverable lease must use atomic ownership changes and fencing/version checks; expiry alone does not prove the original worker stopped. Resume with the same provider operation key within its retention contract, otherwise reconcile.

questions.prompt: Customers report occasional double charges after flaky mobile connections, even though your API supports `Idempotency-Key`. Reviewing the mobile client, you find it creates the key inside the HTTP retry wrapper. Which practices would fix or prevent this class of bug? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use the current timestamp in milliseconds as the key
options.explanation: Wrong. Retries happen at different milliseconds, so each gets a new key, and two users can collide on the same millisecond.

options.text: Generate the key once per logical operation (one tap of Pay) and persist it on the device before the first attempt
options.explanation: Correct. Retries, including after an app restart, then carry the same key, so the server returns the first result instead of charging again.

options.text: Generate a fresh key on each retry, so the server can tell attempts apart
options.explanation: Wrong. That's the bug. Each attempt looks like a new payment to the server, so a retry after a lost response charges twice.

options.text: Have the server store a hash of the request body with the key and reject reuse with a different body
options.explanation: Correct. That doesn't cause double charges, but it catches the opposite bug, one key reused for two different payments, which would otherwise silently return the wrong result.

options.text: Derive the PSP idempotency key deterministically from your payment id, e.g. `pay_123:authorise`
options.explanation: A stable provider key protects the same operation within that provider's retention and parameter contract. Different partial refunds need distinct stable IDs, and ambiguous outcomes after expiry require reconciliation.

questions.workedExample:
Trace the bug:

```
tap Pay
  attempt 1: key A -> charged,
     response lost
  attempt 2: key B -> charged again
```

The server did its job: A and B are different keys. The fix is on the client:

```
tap Pay: save one UUID for all retries
  attempt 1: key K
  attempt 2: key K -> stored result
```

Then layer the other defences:

| Layer | Protects against |
|---|---|
| client key per operation | retries |
| request hash check | key reuse bugs |
| deterministic PSP key | server-side retries |
| UNIQUE ledger ref_id | double posting |

lessons.title: Payment state and asynchronous evidence
lessons.summary: Resolve unknown calls and process authenticated provider events without assuming order.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 2: the payment state machine

```
CREATED -> AUTHORISING -> AUTHORISED
  -> CAPTURING -> CAPTURED -> SETTLED
AUTHORISING -> DECLINED | FAILED
AUTHORISING -> UNKNOWN (timeout)
CAPTURED -> REFUNDING -> (PART)REFUNDED
CAPTURED -> DISPUTED -> WON | LOST
```

- Every transition is a conditional update: a version-checked SQL update of the expected prior state. The transition graph, version check and atomic ledger write together prevent invalid regression; conditional updates alone do not define a correct graph. Track authorisation, capture, refund amounts and disputes separately where they overlap.
- Persist **before** calling out (move to AUTHORISING, *then* call the PSP), so after a crash you know a call may have happened.

### The UNKNOWN state
The PSP call times out. Did the charge happen? You **don't know**, and guessing either way is wrong.

- Don't mark it FAILED and let the customer retry with a new key. That's how double charges happen.
- Do mark it UNKNOWN, then **resolve** it: retry within the PSP's documented idempotency contract with the *same* key, or query the PSP for the payment's status, or wait for the webhook. A background resolver sweeps UNKNOWN payments until resolved, escalating unresolved cases for investigation. An authorisation can be declined, cancelled or expire without settling.

## Deep dive 4: PSP integration and webhooks

PSPs report many outcomes **asynchronously** via webhooks: 3-D Secure completion, captures, refunds, disputes, payouts.

- **Verify using the provider's documented scheme or SDK**. For Stripe this includes the raw body and signed timestamp; check timestamp tolerance and deduplicate event IDs because an authentic event can be replayed within the tolerance.
- **Dedupe by `event_id`**. Insert into `psp_events` with a primary key. If it already exists, return `200` and do nothing. Providers can retry webhook delivery, so duplicates are possible; finite retry windows still permit missed events. Ensure stored but unprocessed events remain discoverable after a crash.
- **Don't trust order.** `charge.refunded` can arrive before `charge.captured`. Either apply events through the state machine, which rejects invalid transitions and retries them later, or treat the webhook as a hint and **fetch the current object** from the PSP API.
- **Acknowledge fast**: write the event durably, return `200`, and process it asynchronously. Slow handlers cause PSP timeouts and redelivery storms.

Multi-PSP setups add **routing**: choose a provider by cost, region, card type and live health, with a circuit breaker for new, unattempted operations. Do not reroute an ambiguous in-flight charge to another PSP: keys are not shared across providers, and the first may already have charged. Resolve its outcome first. Each adapter normalises provider-specific states into your state machine.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A missing payment receipt
> A shop’s receipt printer fails after the payment terminal sends a request. No receipt does not prove the payment failed.
>
> **How it maps:** A timeout leaves the caller uncertain, so it checks the existing payment reference instead of treating every attempt as a new purchase.
>
> **Where it stops:** A person checking a terminal does not implement provider idempotency, durable state or automatic reconciliation.

## Key takeaways
- Persist intent before sending an external operation.
- A timeout means UNKNOWN rather than failure.
- Durably capture signed events, deduplicate and recover processing; fetch current provider state when needed.

## Further reading
- [Idempotent requests (Stripe API docs)](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)
- [The Payment Intents API (Stripe docs)](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/payment-intents)
- [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (Stripe)](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)
- [Stripe webhook contract](https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks)

questions.prompt: Your orchestrator calls the PSP to authorise £80. After 30 s, the call times out with no response. What is the correct next step?

options.text: Mark the payment FAILED and tell the customer to try again
options.explanation: Wrong. The PSP may have authorised the charge. If the customer retries (with a new payment and new key), they may be charged twice, and the first authorisation goes unaccounted for.

options.text: Immediately retry the PSP call with a fresh idempotency key
options.explanation: Wrong. A fresh key tells the PSP it's a *new* operation, so if the first succeeded you've now authorised £160. Retries must reuse the same key.

options.text: Mark it UNKNOWN, then resolve it: retry with the *same* deterministic PSP idempotency key, or query the PSP for the payment by reference, or wait for the webhook. Only then move to AUTHORISED or FAILED
options.explanation: A timeout leaves an ambiguous outcome. Reconcile by reference or retry only within the provider idempotency contract; keys can expire and outcomes may remain unresolved. Authorisation reserves funds and is not itself a settled charge.

options.text: Mark it AUTHORISED optimistically and fix it in reconciliation
options.explanation: Wrong. You might ship goods or start a ride for an unpaid order. Reconciliation is a safety net, not the primary way to learn payment outcomes.

questions.workedExample: The request may never have arrived, may have completed with a lost response, or may still be executing. Persist UNKNOWN. Use a status query/webhook and same-key retries only within the PSP contract. A provider may replay a stored error or remove old keys; unresolved cases need investigation rather than a fresh charge.

questions.prompt: You process PSP webhooks. Which practices are necessary for correctness? Select all that apply.

options.text: Verify each webhook using the provider signature scheme, including any signed timestamp and replay tolerance.
options.explanation: Use the provider SDK with the exact raw-body bytes and signed metadata. Timestamp checks limit old replays; event deduplication is also needed within the permitted time window.

options.text: Insert each event id into a table with a unique key, and skip events already processed
options.explanation: A unique provider/event ID prevents repeated processing when coupled to durable recoverable work and atomic state changes. Finite delivery retries do not guarantee every event arrives.

options.text: Assume events arrive in the order the PSP generated them
options.explanation: Delivery order is not guaranteed. A charge.refunded event can arrive before charge.captured. Store the evidence and apply valid transitions or retrieve current provider state/history.

options.text: Do all processing (ledger postings, emails) synchronously before returning 200
options.explanation: Wrong. Slow handlers exceed the PSP's delivery timeout, causing redeliveries and retry storms. Durably store the event, return 200 quickly, and process asynchronously.

options.text: Route state changes through the same conditional state-machine transitions used by the synchronous API path
options.explanation: Correct. Using one transition function for both paths means a webhook and an API response reporting the same outcome converge, rather than double-posting or regressing state.

questions.workedExample: Verify the provider signature over its required raw bytes and signed timestamp. Atomically persist the event and durable work, acknowledge promptly, then process unprocessed records after crashes. Apply valid state transitions and unique business-operation ledger references in one transaction. Fetch provider state/history when necessary. Different event IDs may describe the same business operation, so event-ID deduplication alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: Payment `pay_555` is AUTHORISED in your database. A `charge.refunded` webhook arrives, but the `charge.captured` webhook hasn't arrived yet. Your state machine only allows `CAPTURED -> REFUNDING/REFUNDED`. What should the handler do?

options.text: Force the status to REFUNDED, since the PSP is the source of truth
options.explanation: Wrong. Skipping CAPTURED means the capture's ledger transaction is never posted, so the refund reverses money the ledger never received.

options.text: Drop the event, since it's an invalid transition
options.explanation: Wrong. The refund really happened. Dropping it guarantees a reconciliation break and money unaccounted for.

options.text: Return 500 so the PSP keeps retrying the webhook forever
options.explanation: Wrong. Failing the webhook risks redelivery storms and, eventually, the PSP giving up. Acknowledge fast once the event is stored.

options.text: Store the event and return 200, then either retry it later once the capture has been applied, or fetch the payment's current state from the PSP and apply the missing transitions in order
options.explanation: Correct. Webhooks can arrive out of order. Treat them as hints: persist them, then converge the local state machine through valid transitions, posting each ledger transaction as you go.

questions.workedExample:
What the PSP actually did:

```
10:00 captured   (webhook delayed)
10:05 refunded   (webhook arrives first)
```

What your handler sees: AUTHORISED, then a refund. Converge it:

1. Insert the event into `psp_events` (dedupe on event_id), return 200.
2. The worker fetches `pay_555` from the PSP API: captured and refunded.
3. Apply `AUTHORISED -> CAPTURED` (post `capture:pay_555`).
4. Apply `CAPTURED -> REFUNDED` (post `refund:re_...`).
5. When the late `charge.captured` webhook arrives, the conditional transition finds the payment already past CAPTURED, and the UNIQUE ref_id stops a second capture posting. It's a no-op.

lessons.title: Double-entry ledger invariants
lessons.summary: Post immutable balanced transactions with precise signs and atomic references.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 3: the double-entry ledger

Double-entry bookkeeping has been the basis of accounting for over 500 years, and it maps beautifully onto software.

- Each **transaction** consists of two or more **entries**. Each entry debits or credits one account.
- **Entries in a transaction sum to zero** per currency:

```formula essential
Σ a_i = 0
where
Σ: add all entries in one transaction for one currency
a_i: signed amount of entry i in that currency's minor units; debits positive and credits negative
i: entry number within the transaction
In words: debits and credits must cancel exactly within each currency, though balance alone does not prove that the economic event is valid.
```

This is an accounting equality; balancing entries alone does not prove the economic event is valid or that cash is conserved.
- Entries are **immutable and append-only**. Mistakes are fixed by posting a *reversing* transaction, never by an UPDATE. History is the audit trail.
- An account's **balance is the sum of its entries**. You can materialise it for speed, but it must always be derivable.

### Worked example
A customer pays £100 for a ride. The driver gets 80% and the platform keeps 20%, and the PSP charges a £1.50 fee. Once the capture settles, one balanced transaction records it:

| Account | Debit | Credit |
|---|---|---|
| PSP clearing (asset) | 98.50 | |
| PSP fees (expense) | 1.50 | |
| Driver payable (liability) | | 80.00 |
| Platform revenue | | 20.00 |
| **Total** | **100.00** | **100.00** |

In storage, a common convention is signed integers in minor units, with debits positive and credits negative:

This local calculation checks the illustrative posting; the database must enforce atomicity and the unique capture reference separately.

```python
# Pence: debits positive, credits negative.
entries = {
    "psp_clearing": 9850,
    "psp_fee_expense": 150,
    "driver_payable": -8000,
    "platform_revenue": -2000,
}
# Zero checks only this balance equality.
print(sum(entries.values()))  # 0
```

Checking the sum-to-zero rule for this transaction:

The two debit entries total £100 and the two credit entries total £100. The fee is recorded separately from gross platform revenue under the stated illustrative accounting policy.

When the PSP pays out, a second transaction debits `bank` and credits `psp_clearing` by 9,850. When the driver is paid, `driver_payable` is debited and `bank` credited by 8,000. Each step balances, and every account's balance explains exactly where the money is.

### Making it consistent
- Write the entries for one transaction **atomically**, in one database transaction, together with the payment state change and an outbox row.
- Put a `UNIQUE` constraint on `ledger_txns.ref_id` (for example `capture:pay_123`), so a re-processed event can't post twice.
- To keep a materialised balance, update `accounts.balance` in the same transaction using optimistic concurrency. Enforce account-type-aware balance limits atomically. With debits-positive storage, credit-normal liabilities naturally have negative stored sums; a blanket `balance >= 0` check would be wrong.

### Hot accounts
Every payment touches `platform_revenue`, so updating its balance row 1,200 times a second serialises on one lock. Options:

- Split it into N sub-accounts, where N is however many you need to spread the writes (`platform_revenue_07` is one of them), and sum them on read.
- Don't materialise balances for hot accounts. Compute them from entries plus periodic snapshots.
- Batch derived balance aggregation for hot accounts, while preserving atomic durable postings for each accepted business transaction.

Purpose-built ledger databases such as TigerBeetle exist precisely because this workload (tiny, contended, must-be-correct transfers) is awkward for general-purpose databases.

## Key takeaways
- Balance debits and credits separately for each currency.
- Post all entries and business-state changes atomically with unique operation references.
- Corrections append reversing entries rather than editing history.

## Further reading
- [Accounting for developers, part I (Modern Treasury)](https://www.moderntreasury.com/journal/accounting-for-developers-part-i)
- [Double-entry bookkeeping (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-entry_bookkeeping)

questions.prompt: A £100 ride is captured. Policy: record £20 gross platform revenue and a separate £1.50 PSP-fee expense; the driver is owed £80. Using debits positive and credits negative in pence, which transaction follows that policy?

options.text: psp_clearing +10000, driver_payable −8000, platform_revenue −2000
options.explanation: Wrong. It balances (10000 − 8000 − 2000 = 0), but it ignores the £1.50 fee. The PSP will only settle £98.50, so psp_clearing would be overstated by 150p and reconciliation would break.

options.text: driver_payable +8000, platform_revenue +2000
options.explanation: These two debit entries total +10,000 pence and lack balancing credits. They also use the wrong normal direction for the stated driver liability and revenue increase. An unbalanced record does not itself prove cash was created.

options.text: psp_clearing +9850, driver_payable −8000, platform_revenue −1850
options.explanation: This balances but nets the fee into revenue, contrary to the stated gross-revenue/separate-expense policy. It is not invalid merely because it balances differently; accounting presentation depends on policy and applicable standards.

options.text: psp_clearing +9850, psp_fee_expense +150, driver_payable −8000, platform_revenue −2000
options.explanation: Correct. 9850 + 150 − 8000 − 2000 = 0. The asset matches what the PSP will actually pay, the fee is an explicit expense, and the platform's gross revenue is £20 (net £18.50 after the fee expense).

questions.workedExample: The stated policy records gross platform revenue and a separate provider-fee expense. The clearing asset is the net amount due from the PSP, the driver payable records the liability, and the fee has its own expense entry. Check per-currency balance and the business policy: an alternative net presentation can balance mathematically while violating this prompt’s policy.

questions.prompt: The £100 ride has not yet been paid out to the driver. Driver share is 80%, platform 20%, PSP fee £1.50. A £30 refund is split pro rata and the PSP retains its fee. With debits positive and credits negative in pence, which transaction records it?

options.text: Update the original capture: psp_clearing +6850, driver_payable −5600, platform_revenue −1400
options.explanation: Wrong. Ledger entries are immutable. A refund is a new transaction, and editing history destroys the audit trail.

options.text: psp_clearing −3000, driver_payable +2400, platform_revenue +600
options.explanation: Correct. £30 leaves via the PSP (a credit to the asset). The amounts owed to the driver and earned by the platform fall by 80% and 20% of £30 (debits). 2400 + 600 − 3000 = 0.

options.text: psp_clearing +3000, driver_payable −2400, platform_revenue −600
options.explanation: Wrong. These signs record *receiving* another £30, which is the opposite of a refund.

options.text: psp_clearing −3000, platform_revenue +3000
options.explanation: Balanced, but it breaks the stated policy: the platform absorbs the whole refund and the driver keeps the full £80.

questions.workedExample: Post a new refund transaction. Credit PSP clearing because funds leave, debit driver payable because less is owed to the unpaid driver, and debit platform revenue for its share. The provider fee remains unchanged under the stated policy. Use a unique refund reference so repeated evidence cannot post twice; do not edit the original capture.

questions.prompt: A new engineer is building the ledger tables. Which rules must the design enforce? Select all that apply.

options.text: Amounts are stored as decimals in major units (23.50) in a float column
options.explanation: Wrong for a binary floating-point column: many decimal fractions are inexact. Use integer minor units or an exact decimal type with specified precision and rounding.

options.text: Entries are append-only. A mistake is corrected by posting a reversing transaction
options.explanation: Correct. History is the audit trail. Updates or deletes would make it impossible to explain how a balance came about.

options.text: Each ledger transaction has a UNIQUE business reference such as `capture:pay_123`
options.explanation: Correct. Re-processing the same event, from a retry or a duplicate webhook, then fails the constraint instead of posting twice.

options.text: A GBP entry and a EUR entry in one transaction may balance each other
options.explanation: Wrong. Sums are meaningful only within one currency. FX is modelled with conversion accounts, so each currency balances on its own.

options.text: The entries in each transaction sum to zero, per currency
options.explanation: Debits and credits must balance within each currency. This accounting equality is necessary but cannot prove the economic event was legitimate or that all external cash was recorded.

questions.workedExample:
Imagine an auditor asks: 'why is the driver payable £812.40?'

- **Append-only** means you can list every entry that produced that balance.
- **Zero-sum transactions** mean every penny on the driver's account is matched by a penny somewhere else.
- **Unique references** mean no event was counted twice.
- **Integer minor units** mean the sum is exact.

For FX, record each side separately:

```
txn fx:123
  customer_gbp   +1000 GBP
  fx_pool_gbp    -1000 GBP
  fx_pool_eur    +1160 EUR
  seller_eur     -1160 EUR
```

The GBP lines sum to zero and the EUR lines sum to zero.

lessons.title: Payment reconciliation and ledger scaling
lessons.summary: Investigate external mismatches and recover cross-shard transfers safely.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 5: reconciliation

Even with perfect code, your view and the outside world's will drift: a webhook never delivered, a manual refund issued in the PSP dashboard, a bank returning a payout. **Reconciliation** is the safety net.

1. Each day, ingest the PSP's **settlement report** (every transaction it settled, its fees and the net payout) and the **bank statement**.
2. **Match** records on references (PSP payment id, payout id) and amounts:
   - internal ledger ↔ PSP report (did every capture we recorded settle, at the amount and fee we expected?)
   - PSP payout ↔ bank deposit (did the money actually arrive?)
3. Unmatched or mismatched items become **reconciliation breaks**: classify them, auto-resolve known patterns (for example, a missed webhook: fetch the object and post the missing transaction), and send the rest to a finance-ops queue.
4. Track reconciliation-break counts and ageing as key health metrics.

Reconciliation checks agreement with the external records available at a point in time. Missing reports, settlement timing and source errors still require investigation; agreement is evidence, not a proof that every economic event is correct.

## Bottlenecks and trade-offs

- **Synchronous vs asynchronous capture**: auth-and-capture in one call is simpler. Separate capture (capture at fulfilment, like a ride ending) reduces refunds but adds a state and an expiry. Authorisation windows depend on network, transaction type and provider rules. For Stripe card charges, inspect `payment_method_details.card.capture_before` rather than hard-coding a seven-day lifetime; delayed capture needs a deadline and an alert.
- **Strong consistency** requires a protocol that orders conflicting operations; one home write region per account is one design, not a requirement. Cross-region consensus is another, with latency and availability trade-offs.
- **Hot accounts** need splitting or batching, as above.
- **Retention vs cost**: keep years of entries online but tiered (hot recent partitions, cold older ones), and archive to immutable object storage.

## Evolving at 10x

- **12,000 payments/s peak**: shard the ledger by account id. Cross-shard transactions (customer on shard A, seller on shard B) become two-phase transfers via a clearing account, or a saga with compensating entries.
- **Event-sourced core**: ledger entries *are* the events. Balances, reports and analytics are projections built by streaming the entries through Kafka.
- **More rails**: bank transfers, open banking and local payment methods each get an adapter into the same state machine and ledger.
- **Risk and fraud** scoring inline before authorisation, using models on device, velocity and history, within a strict latency budget.

## Recovering an account-sharded transfer

At larger scale, the two accounts in one transfer may live on different shards. A local commit on the customer shard cannot atomically prove the seller shard accepted the corresponding entry. Persist a unique transfer identity and durable intent with the first balanced clearing transaction. The destination posts its own balanced clearing transaction once under that identity, and a recoverable relay records progress and retries after crashes.

Individual pending transfers need monitoring: opposite in-flight clearing balances can cancel in aggregate while two customers still have unresolved movements. Compensation also needs coordination. Before refunding the first leg, establish a terminal cancellation at the destination that rejects any delayed second-leg attempt. Otherwise a slow delivery can credit the seller after the customer has been refunded. A clearing-account pattern exposes intermediate state; it does not erase distributed failure.

> **Content gap:** no production capacity benchmark or jurisdiction-complete financial compliance analysis is supplied. The schema, accounting policy and timing targets are illustrative; they are not a complete regulated payments implementation.

## Key takeaways
- Match internal entries, provider settlement and bank receipts by references and amounts.
- Split or snapshot hot accounts without losing the ability to derive balances.
- Cross-shard transfers need durable retry progress and terminal cancellation fencing before compensation.

## Further reading
- [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (Stripe)](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)
- [Idempotent requests (Stripe API docs)](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)
- [The Payment Intents API (Stripe docs)](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/payment-intents)
- [Accounting for developers, part I (Modern Treasury)](https://www.moderntreasury.com/journal/accounting-for-developers-part-i)
- [Two Generals' Problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Generals%27_Problem)
- [Stripe capture expiry](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/place-a-hold-on-a-payment-method)

questions.prompt: During daily reconciliation, the PSP settlement report shows a £45 refund on payment `pay_789` that doesn't appear in your ledger. What is the most likely cause, and the right handling?

options.text: The PSP made an error. Ignore it
options.explanation: A discrepancy needs investigation. The provider or report can also be wrong; do not ignore it or assume the report alone proves the refund occurred. Confirm against available authoritative transaction records.

options.text: Delete payment `pay_789` from the ledger so the totals match
options.explanation: Wrong. Ledgers are append-only. Deleting entries destroys the audit trail and misstates history. Corrections are always new transactions.

options.text: Someone issued a refund directly in the PSP dashboard, or the refund webhook was lost. Raise a break, confirm the refund via the PSP API, and post the missing refund transaction (with a unique ref) to the ledger
options.explanation: Correct. Out-of-band actions and missed webhooks are the classic reasons for breaks. Resolution is to verify against the source of truth and post a correcting, balanced transaction, which can be automated for this known pattern.

options.text: Update the original capture entry from £100 to £55
options.explanation: Wrong. Changing a posted entry rewrites history, and it misrepresents what happened: a £100 capture, then a £45 refund. Post a separate refund transaction.

questions.workedExample: Treat the missing refund as a reconciliation break. Confirm it using available provider transaction evidence and, where needed, audit logs. Then append the missing balanced refund once under its unique reference and agreed allocation policy. If the seller was already paid, recovery may require a receivable instead of reducing an unpaid liability.

questions.prompt: At 1,200 payments/s, every ledger transaction updates the materialised balance of `platform_revenue`. p99 latency spikes, and lock waits on that one row dominate. Which fix keeps the ledger correct?

options.text: Stop recording platform revenue in the ledger
options.explanation: Wrong. Transactions would no longer balance, and revenue would be unauditable. Every movement must be recorded.

options.text: Update the balance asynchronously from a fire-and-forget queue without durable delivery or deduplication
options.explanation: Wrong as stated. Fire-and-forget can lose or duplicate increments, so the balance drifts from the sum of entries. Asynchronous is fine only if it's idempotent and derived from the entries.

options.text: Split the hot account into N sub-accounts (`platform_revenue_00` to `_31`), pick one per transaction, and sum them for reporting. Or don't materialise its balance, and derive it from entries plus periodic snapshots
options.explanation: Correct. Both preserve immutable postings and derivable balances while reducing one-row contention. Shared limits, uneven placement and reporting consistency determine the actual benefit.

options.text: Lower the isolation level to READ UNCOMMITTED
options.explanation: Wrong. Write-write conflicts on one row still serialise on its lock, and dirty reads of balances risk acting on uncommitted data.

questions.workedExample: Every transaction updating one revenue balance row competes for its lock. Splitting posting destinations can distribute contention while preserving balanced transactions and a derivable total. Alternatively, retain entries and compute the balance from a consistent snapshot plus its suffix. Snapshot boundaries, duplicate handling and reporting consistency remain explicit requirements; the number of rows is not a guaranteed speedup.

questions.prompt: At 10x scale the ledger is sharded by account id. A customer's account is on shard A and the seller's on shard B. You implement a transfer as two local transactions through a `clearing` account on each shard. The process crashes after the shard A transaction commits. What makes this safe?

options.text: Nothing. Without two-phase commit, money is lost whenever a crash happens between the steps
options.explanation: Wrong. Durable balanced clearing entries expose a pending transfer. Recoverable delivery, unique destination references and a coordinated cancellation policy can complete or cancel it without a distributed atomic commit.

options.text: Persist transfer intent with shard A’s posting, retry idempotently on B, and track each transfer until completion or fenced cancellation
options.explanation: The durable outbox and unique destination reference make retry recoverable and duplicate-resistant. They do not alone guarantee eventual success or safe compensation; destination cancellation/fencing must prevent a late forward step after reversal.

options.text: Run shard B's step first so the seller is credited before the customer is debited
options.explanation: Wrong. Reordering just moves the crash window. A crash after B commits leaves the seller credited with money nobody was debited for.

options.text: Recompute all balances nightly, which hides the inconsistency
options.explanation: Wrong. Recomputing balances from entries would faithfully reproduce the half-done transfer. The fix is to finish it, not hide it.

questions.workedExample: On shard A atomically post customer +2350, clearing_A -2350 and durable transfer intent. On B atomically post clearing_B +2350 and seller -2350 with a unique transfer reference. A recoverable relay retries; progress requires eventual recovery. Monitor individual transfers, since opposite in-flight balances can cancel in aggregate. Before compensating A, establish a durable terminal cancellation on B that rejects delayed attempts; otherwise a delayed credit could occur after the customer was refunded.

lessons.title: Collaborative editing workload
lessons.summary: Budget operation fan-out and storage using explicit active-editor assumptions.
lessons.body:
Real-time collaborative editing asks for something that sounds impossible. Several people type into the **same** document at the **same** moment, everyone sees their own keystrokes instantly, and everyone ends up with **the same** document, with deterministic conflict handling. Convergence does not guarantee that every competing human intention survives.

The interview centres on one decision, **Operational Transformation (OT) or CRDTs**, and on the architecture that follows from it.

## Requirements

### Functional
- Several users edit a rich-text document at once, and see each other's changes within about 100–200 ms.
- Presence: who's here, plus live cursors and selections.
- Offline editing that merges on reconnect.
- Revision history: view or restore earlier versions, and see who changed what.
- Comments anchored to text ranges, and sharing permissions.

### Non-functional
- **Local echo with no wait**. Your own typing must never wait for the network (optimistic local apply).
- **Convergence**. All replicas reach an identical state once they've seen the same operations.
- **Intention preservation**. Preserve the intended targets under defined edit semantics; no merge algorithm can guarantee every competing human intention.
- **Durability**. An acknowledged edit survives the storage contract’s specified failures.
- High availability, with tolerance for flaky connections.

## Budget edits and recipients separately

An illustrative workload has two million open editors at peak, with one tenth actively typing. If a typist sends five batched edit messages per second, the incoming stream is about one million messages per second. A batch can contain several character operations: distinguish protocol messages from the logical edits inside them.

Each batch must reach the other collaborators on its document. More recipients increase outbound fan-out even when incoming edit traffic is unchanged. Presence, acknowledgements and reconnect synchronization add separate streams; do not hide them inside a single “operations per second” number.

## The busiest document matters

Sharding by document spreads independent documents, but all edits to one document still require its integration and durability work. A fleet average can hide a large shared document with hundreds of participants, large snapshots or a burst of offline edits.

Bound the workload with product limits and test their effects. A viewer relay can distribute broadcasts without adding writable owners. Splitting a document into independently owned sections changes cross-section editing and snapshot semantics, so it needs an explicit contract.

## Keep local response and saved state distinct

Optimistic local echo makes typing visible immediately. A saved indicator must wait for the configured durable acknowledgement. Clients retain unacknowledged edits and retry with stable identities after reconnecting.

The operation log grows with retained edits; its physical size includes synchronization metadata, indexes and copies. Snapshots shorten replay, while compaction trades history detail for storage only when the product permits it. Extending the peak rate over a whole day is a stress model, not a prediction of daily traffic. Measure active editors, document fan-out, batch sizes and the actual daily distribution independently.

## Key takeaways
- Local echo gives immediate typing while durable acknowledgements arrive later.
- Multiply active typists by their batched message rate and collaborator fan-out.
- Snapshot lag and hot-document limits matter beyond fleet-wide totals.

## Further reading

- [CRDTs: the hard parts (Martin Kleppmann)](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2020/07/06/crdt-hard-parts-hydra.html)
- [CRDT resources (crdt.tech)](https://crdt.tech/)
- [Yjs (GitHub)](https://github.com/yjs/yjs)
- [Google Docs sharing limits](https://support.google.com/a/users/answer/9305685?hl=en)

questions.prompt: The edit message rate stays the same, but each document has more collaborators receiving every edit. What changes most directly?

options.text: Outbound fan-out grows even though incoming edit traffic is unchanged
options.explanation: Correct. Each accepted edit must reach more recipients.

options.text: The incoming edit message count necessarily doubles
options.explanation: Wrong. The prompt holds the incoming rate fixed; recipient count changes outgoing work.

options.text: Local echo must wait for every remote recipient
options.explanation: Wrong. Local echo is optimistic and separate from remote delivery and durable acknowledgement.

options.text: Snapshots eliminate all delivery work
options.explanation: Wrong. Snapshots help loading and recovery; active collaborators still need updates.

questions.workedExample: Follow one incoming batch. The owner integrates and persists it, then sends it to the other collaborators. Increasing recipients increases network fan-out. Presence and reconnect synchronization add their own traffic, so a fleet-wide edit average is not enough to size hot documents.

lessons.title: Document contracts and durable ownership
lessons.summary: Route a document to one fenced owner and atomically append each unique edit.
lessons.body:
## API design

This is an illustrative endpoint contract, not a runnable HTTP request. Arrows distinguish responses from submitted fields.

```
GET /v1/docs/{id}
  -> { snapshot, revision, ... }

WS  /v1/docs/{id}/session
  client -> server:
    {type:"op", base_rev: 41,
     client_id, seq: 17, ops:[...]}
    {type:"presence", cursor, selection}
  server -> client:
    {type:"ack", seq: 17, rev: 42}
    {type:"op", rev: 43, author, ops}
    {type:"presence", user, cursor}

GET /v1/docs/{id}/revisions?before=..
POST /v1/docs/{id}/restore {rev}
```

The server atomically records and validates the document-scoped pair `(client_id, seq)` with the edit, making retried submission **idempotent**. A resend after a reconnect is recognised and acknowledged, not applied twice.

## Data model

This is a schema sketch: PK marks the primary key. It omits executable type declarations and migrations.

```
documents(doc_id PK, owner, title,
  latest_rev, latest_snapshot_rev, acl)

doc_ops(doc_id, rev,         PK both
  author, client_id, seq, ops(blob),
  created_at)

doc_snapshots(doc_id, rev,   PK both
  content_ref (blob store), created_at)

named_versions(doc_id, rev, label, by)
```

`(doc_id, rev)` as the op log key gives a **total order per document**. Commit the append atomically with a check of the expected current revision, the current owner epoch and a unique client-operation ID. Revision uniqueness alone does not fence a stale owner or deduplicate retried edits.

## High-level architecture

Follow the arrows as data paths; the drawing is not a deployment specification.

```
 Browsers / apps
      |  WebSocket
      v
+---------------+
| WS gateway    |  auth, routing by
| (stateless)   |  doc_id
+---------------+
      |
      v
+---------------+    +-------------+
| Doc session   |--->| Presence    |
| server (owner |    | pub/sub     |
| per doc_id)   |    | (ephemeral) |
+---------------+    +-------------+
   |         |
   v         v
+--------+ +-----------+
| Op log | | Snapshots |
| (KV/   | | (blob)    |
|  SQL)  | +-----------+
+--------+
```

All sessions for a document route to **one session server**, its owner, chosen by consistent hashing on `doc_id` and held by a lease. The owner keeps the document in memory, orders incoming ops, appends them to the op log, and broadcasts them. If the owner dies, another server takes the lease, loads the latest snapshot, replays ops after it, and clients reconnect.

## Bottlenecks and trade-offs

- **The per-document owner** is a natural serialisation point, which is a bottleneck for very hot documents. Cap editors, and fan out to viewers through a pub/sub tree.
- **Owner failover** creates a short gap, so clients must buffer and resend. The durable store must atomically reject appends from an obsolete owner epoch, in addition to checking the expected revision and deduplicating operation IDs. A unique revision alone cannot reject every stale owner.
- **Large documents** (100-page specs) make snapshots expensive. Split the document into blocks or sections with their own op streams.
- **The cost of OT complexity vs CRDT memory**. Pick based on the offline requirements and the team's appetite for subtle algorithms.

## Key takeaways
- Append the revision, owner epoch and operation-deduplication record atomically.
- A unique revision does not independently fence stale owners.
- Clients retain unacknowledged edits and retry after owner recovery.

## Further reading

- [CRDT resources (crdt.tech)](https://crdt.tech/)
- [Yjs (GitHub)](https://github.com/yjs/yjs)

questions.prompt: Your session server acknowledges ops as soon as they're applied in memory, then writes them to the op log in batches every 2 seconds. A server crash loses the last second of a user's typing, even though their client had shown it as saved. What's the correct fix?

options.text: Write batches every 100 ms instead
options.explanation: Wrong. This shrinks the window but doesn't close it. Any acknowledged-but-unpersisted op can still be lost. The bug is acking before the write is durable.

options.text: Replicate in-memory state to a second server and never write to disk
options.explanation: Wrong. Memory-only replication loses everything if both fail (a rack or power event) and provides no history. You still need a durable log.

options.text: Ack an op only after it's durably appended to the op log. Clients keep unacknowledged ops and resend them after reconnecting, deduplicated by `client_id + seq`
options.explanation: Correct. Acknowledgement must mean 'durable'. Group commit can still batch writes for efficiency, as long as acks wait for the batch. Client-side retention plus idempotent resend covers the in-flight ops.

options.text: Save the full document from the client every 30 seconds
options.explanation: Wrong. Full-document saves from many clients conflict with each other, and that defeats the op-based model. It also doesn't stop acknowledged ops being lost in between.

questions.workedExample: Append the edit, revision, ownership epoch and operation-deduplication record atomically under the selected durability contract; acknowledge only after commit. If the owner crashes before commit, retry; if it crashes after commit but before ack, deduplicate and acknowledge the existing edit. Local echo remains immediate. Group-commit and saved-indicator latency must be measured rather than assumed to be 5 ms or 50–100 ms.

questions.prompt: Each document is owned by one session server via a 10 s lease. Server S1 freezes for 15 s, its lease expires, and S2 takes ownership. S1 unfreezes and keeps accepting ops from clients still connected to it. How do you stop the document's history forking?

options.text: Make the op-log append conditional: `INSERT (doc_id, rev)` must be unique, and carry a fencing token the store checks. S1's appends then fail, so it drops its clients, which reconnect to S2
options.explanation: Correct. The protected store atomically rejects S1’s obsolete ownership epoch even if the next revision is unused. Checking the expected revision and unique operation identity supplies separate ordering and retry guards; revision uniqueness alone is insufficient.

options.text: Trust S1 to check its lease clock before each op
options.explanation: Wrong. A paused process can check, freeze again, and then write. Time-based leases can't guarantee mutual exclusion on their own.

options.text: Let both servers accept ops and merge the two histories later with OT
options.explanation: Wrong. Server-side OT assumes one total order per document. Two divergent server histories, each with acknowledged ops, can't be cleanly reconciled after the fact.

options.text: Use a longer 60 s lease
options.explanation: Wrong. Any lease can be outlived by a pause or partition. It only makes failover slower after genuine crashes.

questions.workedExample: Install the new owner epoch in the protected store before accepting its writes. Atomically verify epoch and expected revision, append the operation and deduplicate its ID. A stale owner must fail even if it guesses an unused revision; uniqueness alone does not fence it. Clients keep unacknowledged edits and reconnect. Durability applies within the explicitly configured storage failure model.
